Trendy means fashionable now and can be superficial, while avant-gardist implies genuine innovation ahead of the mainstream.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is kind of an avant-gardist painter, so her living room is full of strange sculptures.
examples.professional: The agency hired an avant-gardist designer to push the brand away from safe, familiar visuals.
examples.analytical: The avant-gardist refuses the comfort of established forms, treating every convention as a question rather than a rule.

nuance.analogy: Like a scout who runs ahead of the army, testing the ground before anyone else arrives.
nuance.etymology: From French avant-garde, 'advance guard', plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'avant-guardist' with a u, which is a misspelling of the French-derived avant-garde.
Using it as a synonym for 'modern' when it specifically means radical experimentation at the front of a movement.

senses.definition: Rousing from sleep, in a natural or a figurative sense; rousing into activity; exciting.
senses.example: the awakening city

senses.definition: The act of awaking, or ceasing to sleep.
senses.example: The awakening from a nap left her groggy and confused for several minutes.

senses.definition: A revival of religion, or more general attention to religious matters than usual.
senses.example: The camp meeting sparked a spiritual awakening that filled the small town's churches.

senses.definition: Being roused into action or activity.
senses.example: Her awakening to injustice in the factory led her to join the union.

senses.definition: The act of becoming aware of something.

core.definition: A sudden realization or new awareness, often of something important; also the act of waking from sleep.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WAY, the second syllable. The middle syllables are weak, so say kuh-ning rather than separating every sound.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive, as in a new understanding or moral growth. It can be negative in phrases like a rude awakening.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use awakening for a moment of realization, often about social, personal, or political issues, as in a political awakening. A rude awakening means an unpleasant surprise that forces you to face reality. In religious contexts it refers to a revival.

distinctions.note: Revival is a broader term for renewed energy, often religious or cultural. Awakening suggests a sudden shift in consciousness.
Realization is a neutral understanding of a fact. Awakening is more emotional and suggests that your whole view has changed.

examples.everyday: Losing my wallet on vacation was a rude awakening about travel insurance.
examples.professional: The outage was a real awakening for the team about how little we monitor our own pipelines.
examples.analytical: Historians describe the Second Great Awakening as a revival that reshaped American churches in the early nineteenth century.

nuance.analogy: Like turning on the lights in a room you thought was empty.
nuance.etymology: From awake, from Old English onwæcan, 'to wake up', with the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Saying rough awakening instead of rude awakening, which is the fixed phrase.
Using awakening as a verb; the verb is awaken.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to an axon.

core.definition: Relating to an axon, the long nerve fiber that carries signals away from a nerve cell's body.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, 'AK', not on the second as in 'ak-SON'. The final -al reduces to a syllabic l, so it sounds like 'nul' and not like the English word 'nal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a clinical or scientific descriptor with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use axonal in neuroscience, medicine, and biology when describing damage to or growth of the nerve fiber rather than the cell body. Doctors may say 'axonal injury' when explaining a diagnosis to patients. Outside medical or scientific contexts it is almost never used.

distinctions.note: Dendritic refers to the branching fibers that receive signals, while axonal refers to the single long fiber that sends them out.
Neuronal is broader and describes anything relating to neurons, while axonal is specific to the axon part of a neuron.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the nerve damage in my arm is axonal, so it may take months to heal.
examples.professional: The lab report shows axonal loss in the sample, which points to a different mechanism than the demyelination we expected.
examples.analytical: Whether the injury is axonal rather than demyelinating changes the prognosis, because axons regenerate more slowly than myelin repairs.

nuance.analogy: An axonal fiber is like the cable running from a power plant to your house, carrying the signal over long distances.
nuance.etymology: From axon, from Greek axon (axle, axis).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'ak-SOHN-al'.
Confusing axonal with axial, which refers to an axis and has a different meaning.

core.definition: A Seleucid general in 1 Maccabees who fought Judas Maccabeus, defeated him at the battle of Elasa in 160 BC, and later made peace with Jonathan.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, KY, and the final 's' is a 'z' sound. Do not pronounce the 'ch' as in 'church'; it is a hard 'k.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a historical name, and mostly used by readers of the Bible or Jewish and Christian history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this name outside of Bible study, seminary courses or discussions of the Maccabean period. It is used to name the Seleucid commander in 1 Maccabees and in historical works about Judea. Most people will not know who he is without context, so explain him briefly when you mention him.

distinctions.note: Judas Maccabeus was the Jewish leader who led the revolt against the Seleucids, while Bacchides was the Seleucid general who fought against him.
Alcimus was the high priest appointed by the Seleucids, and Bacchides was the general who supported him militarily.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got stuck on Bacchides, the general who keeps showing up in First Maccabees.
examples.professional: In my seminar paper I argue that Bacchides represents the Seleucid attempt to reassert control over Judea after the revolt.
examples.analytical: The narrative of 1 Maccabees 9 presents Bacchides as a shrewd commander whose victory over Judas comes at the cost of the Jewish leader's life.

nuance.analogy: Like a famous enemy commander in a war story, he matters mainly because of the role he plays in the other side's struggle.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ch' as in 'church' rather than as a hard 'k.'
Confusing Bacchides with Alcimus, the high priest, since both are linked to the same Seleucid campaigns.
nuance.biblical_note: Bacchides (Greek Bakchides) is a Seleucid general in 1 Maccabees, which is part of the Apocrypha in Protestant Bibles and the deuterocanonical books in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles. 1 Maccabees 7:8-20 describes him being sent to Judea with Alcimus. 1 Maccabees 9:1-22 records his campaign and his victory over Judas at Elasa, where Judas dies. 1 Maccabees 9:70-73 describes the peace agreement he makes with Jonathan before returning to Syria.

senses.definition: A party held for a woman who is about to be married.

core.definition: A party for a woman about to get married, usually with her close female friends, held shortly before the wedding.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BATCH in this compound, and the last syllable of bachelorette is 'let', rhyming with 'net', not 'ETT' or 'ET'. Avoid stressing the final -ette, which is the most common error.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to playful; it is a lighthearted, celebratory term, often linked with themed outfits, games and teasing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in everyday wedding conversations, for example 'Sarah's bachelorette party is in Miami this year.' These events are often weekend trips with friends, sometimes with matching shirts or sashes. Informal speakers often shorten it to 'bachelorette' or 'bach party.' A natural reply is 'Oh fun, where are you going?'

distinctions.note: The bachelor party is the male version; Americans use the two terms in parallel, so the gender of the guest of honor determines which one you use.
A bridal shower is often a daytime gathering focused on gifts for the bride, while a bachelorette party is typically a night out or weekend trip.

examples.everyday: Sarah's bachelorette party is in Miami, so I'm bringing a nice outfit and a lot of sunscreen.
examples.professional: I'll be out Friday for a bachelorette party, so please send me the notes by Thursday afternoon.
examples.analytical: The bachelorette party reshapes a traditional wedding ritual by centering women's friendships rather than the groom's social world.

nuance.analogy: Like a pre-wedding victory lap with the people who know the bride best.
nuance.etymology: Bachelorette combines bachelor with the French-derived feminine suffix -ette, used for an unmarried woman.
common_mistakes: Saying bachelor party for a woman's event; the female form is bachelorette party.
Stressing the final -ette, as in bach-uh-LET, when the stress in the compound is on BATCH.

conversation.text: Her bachelorette party is in Nashville.
We're doing a spa day for the bachelorette party.
The bachelorette party wore matching T-shirts.

senses.definition: To criticize or malign, especially unfairly or spitefully.
senses.example: Please stop badmouthing your coworkers to the clients; it reflects poorly on you.

core.definition: To criticize someone or something harshly and unfairly, often behind their back.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BAD, with a lighter secondary stress on mouth. The th is voiceless, as in the noun mouth, not the voiced th of the verb to mouth.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes disloyal or spiteful criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use badmouth in casual speech for talking negatively about a boss, coworker, rival or relative, especially when they are not present. It is informal and can sound childish in serious settings. The usual reply is a diplomatic change of subject, such as Let's talk about something else.

distinctions.note: Criticize is neutral and can be constructive, while badmouth implies unfair or spiteful criticism.
Bash is informal and suggests strong public criticism, often in media or online.
Slander is a formal and legal term for spoken false statements that damage reputation, much stronger than badmouth.

examples.everyday: Don't badmouth your brother-in-law at dinner, because it'll get awkward.
examples.professional: Please avoid badmouthing competitors on sales calls and focus on what our product does well.
examples.analytical: Badmouthing a rival in public may win an audience, but it often erodes the speaker's credibility.

nuance.analogy: Like throwing mud on a wall to make the other person look dirty.
nuance.etymology: Compound of bad and mouth, meaning to speak badly of someone.
common_mistakes: Using badmouth for praise or neutral comments: it always implies negative talk.
Pronouncing the verb with the voiced th of the verb mouth, which is /maʊð/, instead of the voiceless th in badmouth.

senses.definition: To cook using an oven, especially baked goods.
senses.example: I baked a delicious cherry pie.

senses.definition: To cook (something) in an oven (for someone).
senses.example: I baked a delicious cherry pie.

senses.definition: To be cooked in an oven.
senses.example: The cake baked at 350°F.

senses.definition: To regularly prepare baked goods.
senses.example: In some cultures, it is expected that a proper housewife should bake.

senses.definition: To smoke marijuana.
senses.example: They sat on the porch and tried to bake before the neighbors came over.

senses.definition: To incorporate into something greater.
senses.example: The team wanted to bake the new security checks into the standard build process.

senses.definition: To heat or dry.
senses.example: The clay baked in the sun.

senses.definition: To be warmed for drying and hardening.
senses.example: The clay baked in the sun.

senses.definition: To dry by heat.
senses.example: They baked the electrical parts lightly to remove moisture.

senses.definition: To be hot.
senses.example: It is baking in the greenhouse.

senses.definition: To cause to be hot.
senses.example: The desert sun will bake the parking lot until the asphalt softens by noon.

senses.definition: To fix (lighting, reflections, etc.) as part of the texture of an object to improve rendering performance.
senses.example: In the game engine, we bake the shadows into the textures to speed up rendering.

senses.definition: The act of cooking food by baking.
senses.example: A slow bake at low heat keeps the cheesecake creamy and prevents cracks.

senses.definition: Any food item that is baked, such as a pastry.
senses.example: bake pan

senses.definition: A social event at which food (such as seafood) is baked, or at which baked food is served.
senses.example: an oyster bake on the shore

senses.definition: A small, flat (or ball-shaped) cake of dough eaten mainly in Barbados, similar in appearance and ingredients to a pancake but fried (or sometimes roasted).
senses.example: For breakfast we ordered bake and saltfish, a Barbadian favorite with fried dough.

core.definition: To cook food, usually bread, cakes, or cookies, in an oven using dry heat.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable that rhymes with 'cake' and 'make'. Keep the vowel as a long 'ay' and the final 'k' clear, without adding a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Positive and homey. Baking suggests care, comfort, and home cooking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bake for cooking food in an oven, especially sweets and bread, and also for casseroles and some main dishes. In a restaurant conversation, you might ask 'Is the bread baked here?' In everyday talk, 'I'm going to bake cookies' is natural, while 'I'm going to roast cookies' sounds wrong.

distinctions.note: Roasting usually refers to meat and vegetables cooked at high heat, while baking is the usual word for breads, cakes, and most casseroles.
Broiling cooks food with direct heat from above, usually for a short time, while baking uses an oven at a steady temperature.

examples.everyday: I'm going to bake a batch of cookies tonight if you want to come over.
examples.professional: Could you bake a small test batch of the new muffin recipe before we commit to the bulk order?
examples.analytical: To bake bread is to transform raw ingredients through heat, a process that changes both texture and flavor in ways cooks have studied for centuries.

nuance.analogy: Baking is like a slow, steady warm-up for food: the oven surrounds it with dry heat until it sets, rises, and browns.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bacan, meaning to cook in dry heat.
common_mistakes: Using roast for baked goods, such as saying 'roasted cookies' instead of 'baked cookies'.
Confusing bake with the noun baker when describing a person; 'I'm a baker' is correct, not 'I'm a bake'.

bake.etymology: From Middle English *baken*, from Old English *bacan* (“to bake”), from **bakan*, from Proto-Germanic **bakaną* (“to bake”), from Proto-Indo-European **bʰeh₃g-* (“to roast, bake”).

conversation.text: I'm going to bake cookies for the party.
She bakes bread every weekend and gives some to the neighbors.
Bake the cake for about thirty minutes.

senses.definition: An uncultivated ridge formed in the open field system, caused by the action of plowing.
senses.example: Farmers left a balk of unplowed earth between the fields to mark the boundary.

senses.definition: The wall of earth at the edge of an excavation.
senses.example: The archaeologists left a balk of soil standing so they could read the layers.

senses.definition: Beam, crossbeam; squared timber; a tie beam of a house, stretching from wall to wall, especially when laid so as to form a loft, "the balks".
senses.example: The old barn had a balk spanning the walls, where the family stored hay.

senses.definition: A hindrance or disappointment; a check.
senses.example: Her sudden resignation was a serious balk to the project's launch.

senses.definition: A sudden and obstinate stop.
senses.example: The mule came to a balk at the creek and would not move.

senses.definition: A motion used to deceive the opponent during a serve.
senses.example: The server's balk fooled the receiver, who lunged too early.

senses.definition: The area of the table lying behind the line from which the cue ball is initially shot, and from which a ball in hand must be played.
senses.example: He placed the cue ball deep in the balk to block his rival's shot.

senses.definition: The area of the table lying behind the baulk line.
senses.example: He placed the cue ball deep in the balk to block his rival's shot.

senses.definition: The rope by which fishing nets are fastened together.
senses.example: The fisherman tied the net to the balk before hauling in the catch.

senses.definition: A deceptive motion.
senses.example: With a quick balk of his shoulders, the boxer fooled his opponent completely.

senses.definition: An illegal motion by the pitcher, intended to deceive a runner.
senses.example: The umpire called a balk when the pitcher faked a throw to first base.

senses.definition: To be unwilling to do something; to refuse to proceed or do or allow something, either in general or only temporarily.
senses.example: balked at paying a day's wages for a pencil; he said he would buy her one, but when he saw the price, he balked

senses.definition: To stop short and refuse to go on or do something (such as jump).
senses.example: The horse balked.

senses.definition: To move fitfully, stopping frequently.
senses.example: The nervous donkey would balk and stall, then lurch forward again along the trail.

senses.definition: To leave or make a balk or balks (ridges) in; to leave a ridge in by leaving partly unploughed.
senses.example: He would balk the north field each spring, leaving ridges of unplowed earth between rows.

senses.definition: To stop, check, block (by or as if by an obstacle); to hinder, impede, thwart.
senses.example: Heavy snow balked our plans to drive to the coast this weekend.

senses.definition: To disappoint, frustrate, or check.
senses.example: to balk expectation

senses.definition: To make a balk, a deceptive motion to deceive another player.
senses.example: In the drill, the player balked to his left, then drove right past the defender.

core.definition: To suddenly refuse or hesitate to do something you are reluctant about, often because you dislike it or doubt it.

pronunciation.tip: The L is silent, so the word rhymes with talk and walk. In General American the vowel is the open AW of caught, not the short a of back.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It suggests stubborn reluctance, but it is less harsh than flatly refusing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use balk mostly in the phrase balk at, as in balk at the price or balk at the idea. It sounds natural in work, family and shopping situations, and it is slightly more vivid than simply saying no. In baseball, a balk is an illegal motion by a pitcher, so Americans may also think of that sport when they hear the word.

distinctions.note: Hesitate means pausing before deciding, while balk means resisting once something is asked of you.
Refuse is direct and complete, but balk suggests reluctance and a stop short of full compliance.
Object means stating that you disagree, while balk describes the resistance itself, often without an explicit protest.

examples.everyday: I wanted to go hiking, but my brother balked at the idea of getting up at five.
examples.professional: The finance team balked at approving the budget until we provided a detailed cost breakdown.
examples.analytical: Kant's ethics balks at any justification of lying, even when a lie might save a life.

nuance.analogy: A horse that plants its feet and will not step over a fence is balking.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English balke, a ridge or beam; the verb sense developed from the idea of stopping short at an obstacle.
common_mistakes: Saying the L, as in bolk; the L is silent.
Using balk to without a preposition; the natural form is balk at doing something.
Confusing balk with talk or bulk in spelling and pronunciation.

balk.etymology: From Middle English *balke*, from Old English *balca*, either from or influenced by Old Norse *bálkr* (“partition, ridge of land”), from Proto-Germanic **balkô*.

senses.definition: Not classical or pure.
senses.example: Scholars criticized the poet's barbarous Latin, which ignored classical grammar entirely.

senses.definition: Uncivilized, uncultured.
Mercilessly or impudently violent or cruel, savage.
senses.example: The dictator's barbarous treatment of prisoners shocked the entire international community.

senses.definition: Like a barbarian, especially in sound; noisy, dissonant.
senses.example: The neighbors' barbarous music rattled our windows until well past midnight.

core.definition: Extremely cruel, brutal, or savage, in a way that shocks people. Also used for something very crude or uncivilized.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending is the weak syllable 'us,' not 'OH-us.' The middle syllable is nearly silent, so say it as 'BAR-bruss' with a light r sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes cruelty or crudeness that people find shocking, so it is strong and should be used with care.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use barbarous mostly in serious writing, news commentary, or a formal complaint, such as 'barbarous treatment of prisoners.' In everyday talk, people usually say 'brutal,' 'cruel,' or 'savage' instead. Calling a minor annoyance barbarous sounds exaggerated or dramatic.

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning, but barbaric is more common in everyday American speech and barbarous sounds more formal and bookish.
Brutal focuses on physical force and harshness, while barbarous adds a sense of moral outrage at a lack of civilization.

examples.everyday: The way they treated those stray dogs was barbarous, and the whole neighborhood was furious.
examples.professional: Cutting the QA budget in the middle of the release was a barbarous decision, and we're still cleaning up the mess.
examples.analytical: Hobbes described life without a common power as solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short, a barbarous condition that civil society exists to escape.

nuance.analogy: Barbarous is like a tree that has been cut down with no care for the rest of the forest: it shows a shocking lack of restraint.
nuance.etymology: From Greek barbaros, meaning foreign or non-Greek speaking, an imitation of unintelligible speech.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'bar-BAIR-us' with stress on the second syllable.
Using barbarous for mild rudeness; it is a strong word for serious cruelty or crudeness.

barbarous.etymology: Late Middle English, from Latin *barbarus* (“foreigner, savage”), from Ancient Greek *βάρβαρος* (“foreign, strange”).

senses.definition: Obscene; filthy; unchaste.
senses.example: The bawdy tale was too filthy for a children's storytelling hour.

senses.definition: Sexual in nature and usually meant to be humorous but considered rude; ribald.
senses.example: The comedy club's bawdy jokes made the audience laugh until they cried.

senses.definition: A bawdy or lewd person.
senses.example: The old sailor was a bawdy who sang filthy songs in every port.

core.definition: Earthy and humorously rude, dealing with sex or the body in a playful rather than mean way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with the aw vowel of 'law'. The word has two syllables, and the second is a clear dee, not 'dih'.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative to playful; it suggests lewd humor that is entertaining but unrefined.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bawdy for humorous sexual or crude content, such as a raunchy comedy or a dirty joke at a party. In professional settings it sounds too strong, so people say 'inappropriate' or 'off color' instead. 'Off color' is the everyday American phrase for a joke that's crude.

distinctions.note: Ribald means nearly the same thing but sounds more literary; bawdy is more common in everyday speech.
Off color is the common American idiom for a crude joke, and it is more casual and widely understood at work.

examples.everyday: My uncle always told bawdy jokes at Thanksgiving, and my aunt would just roll her eyes.
examples.professional: I wouldn't use that bawdy punchline in the team presentation, since it might make people uncomfortable.
examples.analytical: Chaucer's bawdy tales show how medieval humor could be both earthy and morally pointed.

nuance.analogy: Bawdy humor is like a comedian who knows exactly how far to push the crowd before they gasp.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English bawdy, from Old French baud, meaning 'gay' or 'merry'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'bow-dy' with the vowel of 'bow' instead of the aw of 'law'.
Using bawdy for simply sexy or romantic; it means rude and humorous.

senses.definition: Each in a string of small balls making up the rosary or paternoster.
A small, round object.
senses.example: beads of sweat

senses.definition: A small, round object with a hole to allow it to be threaded on a cord or wire, particularly for decorative purposes.
Various small, round solid objects.
A small drop of water or other liquid.
senses.example: beads of sweat

senses.definition: A bubble, in spirits.
A small, round ball at the end of a barrel of a gun used for aiming.
senses.example: She drew a bead on the target and fired.

senses.definition: Knowledge sufficient to direct one's activities to a purpose.
senses.example: We now have a bead on the main technical issues for the project

senses.definition: A ridge, band, or molding.
A rigid edge of a tire that mounts it on a wheel; tire bead.
A decorative, convex, rounded profile (often a half-circle) cut into an edge or surface of wood, typically defined by a narrow, deep channel called a quirk.
A narrow molding with semicircular section.
(dated) A glassy drop of molten flux, as borax or microcosmic salt, used as a solvent and color test for several mineral earths and oxides, as of iron, manganese, etc. before the blowpipe.
senses.example: the borax bead; the iron bead, etc.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To form into a bead.
senses.example: The raindrops beaded on the car's waxed finish.

senses.definition: To apply beads to.
senses.example: She spent the morning beading the gown.

senses.definition: To cause beads to form on (something).

core.definition: A small, round object, often with a hole for stringing; also a small drop of liquid, such as sweat.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long e, as in 'see', so the word rhymes with 'need' and 'seed'. Do not shorten it to the vowel in 'bed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is literal and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bead most in craft and jewelry talk, like 'glass beads' or 'a bead necklace', and in everyday descriptions like 'beads of sweat on his forehead'. The plural form is used for most everyday expressions. In religious contexts, a rosary bead is a specific use, so context matters.

distinctions.note: A pearl is a natural or cultured gem formed in an oyster, while a bead is usually made of glass, wood, plastic or stone.
A drop is a general word for a small amount of liquid, while a bead specifically suggests a round, clinging drop, like sweat or dew.

examples.everyday: There were beads of sweat on his forehead after the long hike up the trail.
examples.professional: The jewelry supplier shipped the wrong color of glass beads for the spring line.
examples.analytical: Medieval devotion often used beads to count repeated prayers, turning repetition into a form of meditation.

nuance.analogy: A bead is like a small seed of meaning: one unit that gains value when placed in a string.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bede, prayer, because prayers were counted on strings of beads.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'bed' with a short e.
Saying a beads when you mean one bead; use a bead or several beads.

bead.etymology: From Middle English *bede* (“a prayer”), also “a bead for counting prayers” in *a peire of bedes*, from Old English *bedu*, *bed*, *ġebed* (“a request, entreaty, prayer”), from **bedu*, **bed*, **gabed*, from Proto-Germanic **bedō*, **bedą*.

senses.definition: The quality of being (especially visually) attractive, pleasing, fine or good-looking; comeliness.
Someone who is beautiful.
senses.example: Brigitte Bardot was a renowned beauty.

senses.definition: Those aspects or elements that make someone or something beautiful.
senses.example: Many mathematicians say the beauty of a proof lies in its simplicity and elegance.

senses.definition: Something that is particularly good or pleasing.
senses.example: What a goal! That was a real beauty!

senses.definition: An excellent or egregious example of something.
senses.example: He got into a fight and ended up with two black eyes – two real beauties!

senses.definition: The excellence or genius of a scheme or decision.
senses.example: The beauty of the deal is it costs nothing!

senses.definition: Beauty treatment; cosmetology.
senses.example: a hair and beauty salon

senses.definition: Thanks!
senses.example: You finished the report before lunch? Beauty, thanks so much for handling that!

senses.definition: Cool!
senses.example: It's the long weekend. Beauty!

senses.definition: Of high quality, well done.
senses.example: He made a beauty pass through the neutral zone.

core.definition: The quality that makes a person, place or thing pleasing to look at; attractiveness, or a person or thing that has it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -y is a light 'ee'. In casual American speech the t between vowels is a flap, so it sounds close to 'BYOO-dee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It can sound shallow when it refers only to physical appearance, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use beauty in both everyday and literary talk, for nature, art, a person's appearance or the appeal of an idea. 'She's a beauty' is informal praise for a person or a car. The interjection 'Beauty!' means 'great!' and is informal, mostly used by friends.

distinctions.note: Beauty is a more general and elevated quality, while attractiveness is looser and often describes appeal to a particular person.
Beauty is about visual or aesthetic qualities, while charm is about pleasing manner and personality.

collocations: beauty is in the eye of the beholder

examples.everyday: The Blue Ridge Mountains in the fall have a beauty that takes your breath away.
examples.professional: Our design review focuses on usability first, since beauty means little if customers cannot complete their tasks.
examples.analytical: Augustine located the beauty of creation in its order and proportion, which he read as pointing beyond itself to the Creator.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-cut diamond, its appeal comes from both its form and the light it catches.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English beaute, from Old French beauté, from Latin bellitas (prettiness), from bellus (fine, pretty).
common_mistakes: Using beauty as an adjective, as in 'She is very beauty'; say 'very beautiful' or 'a beauty'.
Stressing the second syllable or saying it as the French 'bo-tay' sound.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture beauty often means pleasantness or the splendor of God's presence, not just physical looks. The Hebrew no'am (pleasantness, delight) appears in Psalm 27:4, where the psalmist asks to behold the beauty of the LORD. Proverbs 31:30 (RSV) warns that charm is deceitful and beauty is vain, so the woman who fears the LORD is the one to be praised.

beauty.etymology: From Middle English *bewty*, *bewte*, *beaute*, *bealte*, from Anglo-Norman and Old French *beauté* (early Old French spelling *biauté*), from Vulgar Latin **bellitātem* (“beauty”), from Latin *bellus* (“beautiful, fair”); see *beau*.

senses.definition: A competition in which participants compete for a determination that one is the most physically attractive.
A tender in which bidders are ranked according to some (known or secret) criteria.
senses.example: The city ran a beauty contest, ranking developers' bids against undisclosed criteria for the land.

core.definition: A competition in which entrants are judged mainly on physical attractiveness, or a process in which choices are made by guessing what others will pick.

pronunciation.tip: The noun 'contest' stresses its first syllable (KAHN-test), unlike the verb 'con-TEST'. The vowel in KAHN is the open 'ah' used in General American, the same as in 'cot'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or critical when it suggests judging people only by looks or choosing things by image rather than substance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for pageants, but also in business and politics to criticize a process that rewards appearance over performance. In finance, the term comes from John Maynard Keynes and describes investors who pick what others will favor. A neutral alternative for a formal bidding process is 'competitive bidding' or 'request for proposals'.

distinctions.note: A pageant usually includes talent, interviews and ceremony, while beauty contest focuses on looks, and the phrase is often used critically.
A popularity contest judges who people like, while a beauty contest judges appearance or the image something projects.

examples.everyday: I'm not going to watch that beauty contest on TV, it's all about looks.
examples.professional: The procurement team ran the vendor selection like a beauty contest, scoring slide decks rather than delivery records.
examples.analytical: Keynes compared investing to a newspaper beauty contest in which success goes to those who guess what others will pick, not to the faces they find most beautiful.

nuance.analogy: Like a hiring process that judges the headshot more than the work.
nuance.etymology: Beauty plus contest, from Latin contestari (to call as witness, to dispute).
common_mistakes: Using beauty contest in a neutral sense for any competition; the phrase suggests judging by appearance.
Stressing the second word as kon-TEST, which is the verb pattern.

senses.definition: A command, bidding; sometimes also, an authoritative request; now usually in the phrase at the behest of and at one's behest.

core.definition: A formal command or request from someone with authority, usually used in the phrases at someone's behest or at the behest of.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, HEST, which rhymes with 'best.' The first syllable is a short, unstressed 'bih.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, because a behest implies that someone with authority is directing action, sometimes without much choice for the person obeying.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use behest almost only in set phrases such as 'at the behest of' in news, legal writing, or formal speech. It sounds stiff in casual talk, so people usually say 'at someone's request' or 'because someone asked.' A natural reply to 'I did it at the boss's behest' is 'Okay, I figured it was coming from above.'

distinctions.note: A request can come from anyone, while a behest comes from someone with authority, and it often sounds more like a command.
Order is common and direct, while behest is formal and suggests that the command came from someone important.

examples.everyday: The neighbors asked me to move my car, and I did it at the building manager's behest.
examples.professional: The migration was rolled out at the CTO's behest, even though the team had raised concerns about the timeline.
examples.analytical: Hobbes treats obedience to the sovereign's behest as the foundation of civil order, since the sovereign alone decides what the law requires.

nuance.analogy: A behest is like a directive from the top of an org chart: it comes down with authority, and everyone below is expected to act on it.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English behest, from Old English behæs, meaning a vow or command, from behatan 'to promise.'
common_mistakes: Using behest as a synonym for any request in casual speech, where request is more natural.
Writing 'on behest' or 'by behest' instead of the standard phrase 'at the behest of.'

behest.etymology: From Middle English *biheste*, from Old English *behǣs* (“vow, promise”), from **bihaisi*, from **bi-* + **haisi*, from Proto-Germanic **haisiz*, from **haitaną* (“to command”).

senses.definition: To befit, to suit.
senses.example: It ill behooves my mother to complain.

senses.definition: To be necessary for (someone).
To be in the best interest of; to benefit.
senses.example: It behooves every data team to document its models before deploying them.

senses.definition: To be needful, meet or becoming.
senses.example: It behooves a minister to speak with humility when addressing a grieving congregation.

core.definition: To be proper, necessary or to one's advantage; to be the duty of someone to do something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, HOOV. The vowel is the oo of 'move,' and the word ends with a v, so do not say 'behoof' with an f.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly formal. It sounds polite, measured and slightly old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'behoove' is used almost only in the phrase 'it behooves you (or us) to,' usually in formal writing, letters, editorials or speeches. In casual talk, Americans say 'you should' or 'it's a good idea to.' The spelling is 'behoove' in American usage, while 'behove' is the more common British form in older texts. Using it in conversation can sound preachy or dated.

distinctions.note: 'Should' is the everyday word for advice or obligation. 'Behoove' is more formal and suggests the action is required for propriety or advantage.
'Ought' expresses moral obligation. 'Behoove' focuses on what is fitting or advantageous, and it is less common in speech.

examples.everyday: It behooves you to wear a warm coat, because the wind is brutal today.
examples.professional: It behooves us to double-check the sample size before we publish these results.
examples.analytical: It behooves the reader of Scripture to attend to the historical context of each passage before drawing theological conclusions.

nuance.analogy: 'Behoove' is like a coat that fits the occasion: it is the right thing to wear, and it suits the situation.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English behoven, related to behove, from Old English behofian, to be necessary.
common_mistakes: Using 'behoove' with a direct object and no 'it' (for example, 'This behooves me' is fine, but 'I behoove to go' is wrong).
Spelling it 'behove' in American writing, where 'behoove' is the usual form.

behoove.etymology: From Middle English *behoven*, *bihoven* (“to be necessary, requisite; to be compelled or required”), from Old English *behōfian* (“to need; to be necessary”), from Proto-Germanic **bihōfōną* (“to benefit, behove, need”), ultimately from…

senses.definition: Somebody who gives a gift, often money to a charity.
senses.example: anonymous benefactor

senses.definition: Someone who performs good or noble deeds.
senses.example: The local benefactor quietly paid for the children's hospital wing last year.

core.definition: A person who gives money or other help, especially to a school, hospital, museum, or charity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BEN. The final syllable is a reduced 'er' sound, so say 'ter' lightly, not as a full 'tor'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes a generous, admirable person, sometimes with a slight sense of prestige.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use benefactor for someone who donates a lot of money to a cause, especially in news about universities, hospitals, and museums. You might say 'She was a major benefactor of the art museum.' It sounds slightly formal; for a friend who helped you, 'You're a lifesaver' would be more natural.

distinctions.note: A donor is anyone who gives; a benefactor is usually a major, often long-term supporter, sometimes honored by name.
A beneficiary receives the benefit; a benefactor gives it.

examples.everyday: My aunt was a big benefactor of the animal shelter, and they named a room after her.
examples.professional: Our biggest benefactor just gave the hospital a grant for the new pediatric wing.
examples.analytical: The benefactor's role raises questions about whether private wealth should shape public institutions.

nuance.analogy: Like a sponsor who keeps the lights on so the show can go on.
nuance.etymology: From Latin benefactor, from benefacere, 'to do good'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (ben-uh-FAK-ter) instead of the first.
Using 'benefactor' for any helper; it usually refers to someone who gives money or resources.
Mispronouncing the final syllable with a strong 'or' sound instead of a reduced 'er'.

benefactor.etymology: From Middle English *benefactor*, borrowed from Medieval Latin *benefactor* (“he who bestows a favor”), from Latin *benefaciō* (“benefit someone”), from *bene* (“good”) + *faciō* (“do, make”).

senses.definition: In a beseeching manner.

core.definition: In a pleading, urgent way, with a look or tone that begs for help or mercy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, which is the long 'ee' vowel, and the final syllables are reduced. Don't stress the first syllable as 'BEE-suh-cheeng-lee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to emotional. It describes a visual or vocal appeal, often sad or desperate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in fiction, memoirs, or descriptive writing, such as 'she looked at me beseechingly.' In casual speech, people say 'with pleading eyes' or 'looking desperate.' It is rare outside literature and is a formal way to describe someone's manner.

distinctions.note: 'Pleadingly' is similar but more common in everyday writing. 'Beseechingly' is more formal and literary, with a stronger sense of urgency.
'Imploringly' suggests a more intense, almost desperate appeal. 'Beseechingly' is gentler and more restrained.

examples.everyday: My little brother looked up at me beseechingly, asking if he could have one more cookie.
examples.professional: The junior analyst glanced at the director beseechingly, hoping someone would step in to help with the outage.
examples.analytical: The narrator watches the father beseechingly, as if the boy's silence could be broken by pure need.

nuance.analogy: Speaking beseechingly is like holding out an open hand: the gesture asks for something without saying it fully.
nuance.etymology: From beseech, 'to implore,' plus the adverb suffix -ingly, from Middle English besechen.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
Spelling the adverb as 'beseechingly' but pronouncing the 'ch' as 'k' or 'sh.'
Using it in casual speech where 'pleadingly' or 'with pleading eyes' would sound more natural.

senses.definition: An instance of something being bitten.
senses.example: Repeated biting by the puppy had left the cable's insulation cracked and exposed.

senses.definition: A bite-sized snack.
senses.example: She packed cheese and apple bitings in the kids' lunches for the hike.

senses.definition: Causing a stinging sensation.
senses.example: a biting wind

senses.definition: Cutting or incisive.
senses.example: a biting criticism

senses.definition: Tending to bite.
senses.example: a biting insect

core.definition: Sharply cold or stinging, or cutting and critical in tone. Used for weather or remarks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a clear long 'eye' vowel and a short, reduced -ing ending. Do not say 'BY-teeng'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing remarks or criticism; neutral to unpleasant when describing weather.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'biting wind' or 'biting cold' in weather reports and everyday talk. It is also common for sharp remarks, as in 'a biting comment.' Use it when someone's words cut into you, not for mild disagreements. In fact, 'bite-sized' is a separate adjective for food.

distinctions.note: Stinging suggests a sharp hurt or pain, while biting suggests a cutting, incisive edge, especially in criticism or cold weather.
Cutting is similar but stronger in emotional force; biting often describes wit or tone more than harsh intent.

examples.everyday: It's a biting cold out there, so wear a hat and gloves.
examples.professional: Her feedback in the code review was direct and biting, but it was useful because it named the real problem.
examples.analytical: The essay's biting irony exposes the gap between the author's stated ideals and his actual practice.

nuance.analogy: Like a cold wind that finds the gap in your coat, biting language finds the weak spot in your argument.
nuance.etymology: From bite (Old English bītan) with the participial suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Using 'biting' for taste; say 'bitter' or 'sharp' for flavors.
Confusing biting (sharp) with bite-sized (a snack size).

senses.definition: Relating to creative work.
senses.example: black-collar worker

senses.definition: Relating to coalminers and oil workers.
(rare) Of or pertaining to employment in the black market; that is, to engagement in illicit trade or distribution of untaxed goods and services.
senses.example: The investigators uncovered a black-collar network selling untaxed cigarettes across three counties.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) Relating to the clergy.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Of a worker or work: relating to creative or artistic labor. This is a rare, inconsistently used term.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, BLACK, as with most hyphenated adjectives. Collar has a short second syllable with an r you should pronounce, and the vowel in kah is the American cot vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the creative sense; negative when it refers to illegal black-market work.
nuance.usage_note: Black-collar is rare and not standardized, so people may use it differently. In American English, white-collar and blue-collar are the common terms, and you will rarely hear black-collar in conversation. If you meet it, check the context: it may describe creative workers or illegal, off-the-books trade. For illegal dealings, Americans usually say black market or off the books.

distinctions.note: White-collar refers to office and professional work, the common American term, while black-collar is rare and used in different ways.
Blue-collar refers to manual or industrial work, such as factory or construction labor, which is a different category.
Gray-collar is a common American term for technical or IT workers, who mix office and hands-on work.

examples.everyday: My cousin has a black-collar job, designing album covers and posters for bands.
examples.professional: Our hiring manager calls the studio's illustrators black-collar workers, but HR never uses the term.
examples.analytical: The label black-collar is used loosely, so scholars should define it before comparing it with white-collar work.

nuance.analogy: Like a nickname that means different things in different groups, its meaning depends on who uses it and in what setting.
nuance.etymology: Formed by analogy with white-collar and blue-collar; its specific senses are not standardized.
common_mistakes: Assuming black-collar always means illegal, when some uses refer to creative work.
Stressing the second word, collar, instead of the first word, black.

senses.definition: A blunder, an error.
A filmed or videotaped outtake that has recorded an amusing accident or mistake.
senses.example: The DVD extras include a blooper reel with actors flubbing their lines.

senses.definition: The Vietnam-era M79 grenade launcher (due to its distinctive report).
senses.example: Soldiers called the M79 grenade launcher a blooper because of its loud pop.

senses.definition: A fly ball that is weakly hit just over the infielders.
senses.example: The shortstop dove for the blooper but could not reach it in time.

senses.definition: A gaff-rigged fore-and-aft sail set from and aft of the aftmost mast of a square-rigged ship; a spanker.
senses.example: The sailors hoisted the blooper to catch more wind off the stern.

senses.definition: A radio which interferes with other radios, causing them to bloop (squeal loudly).
senses.example: The cheap walkie-talkie was a blooper that squealed whenever the neighbors used their radios.

core.definition: An embarrassing error or blunder, often made in public or on camera.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a long oo as in 'moon'. The final -er is an unstressed American r sound, not a full 'pair' sound.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or humorous. It names a mistake that is embarrassing but usually not serious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'blooper' for a funny public mistake: a sports error, a TV slip or a speech gaffe. 'Bloopers' often refers to outtakes shown after movies or on TV. A natural response is 'Oh no, that was a blooper!' or 'Everybody has bloopers.' In serious settings, say 'error' or 'mistake'.

distinctions.note: 'Blunder' is a serious, careless error; 'blooper' is usually lighter, often public and funny.
A 'gaffe' is a social faux pas, such as saying something rude; a blooper is a mistake in action or speech on stage, TV or in sports.
'Error' is neutral and general; 'blooper' is informal and usually noticeable to an audience.

examples.everyday: Did you see that blooper where the anchor read the wrong score?
examples.professional: Let's fix that blooper in the slide deck before the client call.
examples.analytical: The blooper genre reveals how audiences enjoy seeing polished professionals stripped of their composure.

nuance.analogy: Like a dropped ball in the middle of a great play, the mistake is visible to everyone.
common_mistakes: Using 'blooper' for a serious professional error; in the US it sounds too light.
Saying 'blue-per' with a diphthong; the stressed vowel is a single long oo.

senses.definition: Having the qualities of a bog; i.e. dank, squishy, muddy, and full of water and rotting vegetation.
senses.example: The edge of the woods led out onto a noisome, boggy fen, a paradise for mosquitos and small frogs.

core.definition: Wet, soft and muddy, like a bog, so that the ground sinks or squelches under your feet.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -y is a clear long ee. Bog has the short cot vowel, not the oh of 'boat'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes unpleasant wet ground, often a warning about walking through a field or trail.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use boggy for wet land on hiking trails, farms, golf courses and in weather reports. It is ordinary, descriptive vocabulary. For a large wetland, Americans often say swamp or marsh rather than bog.

distinctions.note: Marshy suggests grassy wetland with shallow water; boggy suggests soft, spongy ground that sinks underfoot.
Swampy suggests standing water and trees or dense vegetation; boggy suggests peat-like softness.

examples.everyday: Wear boots, the trail is boggy after all that rain.
examples.professional: The site is too boggy for heavy equipment, so we'll schedule the excavation for July.
examples.analytical: The boggy soil of the valley shaped both the settlement patterns and the early agricultural economy.

nuance.analogy: Like a wet sponge that squishes and sinks when you step on it, boggy ground gives way under your weight.
nuance.etymology: From bog (soft wet ground, from Irish or Scottish Gaelic bog meaning soft) plus the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using boggy for a dry, sandy place or a general swamp with deep water; boggy means soft and wet.
Pronouncing the first syllable with a long oh as in 'boag'.

senses.definition: Resembling, having the appearance or consistence of, or relating to bone; osseous.
senses.example: The doctor said the X-ray showed bony growths along the edge of the knee.

senses.definition: Full of bones.
With little flesh; skinny, thin.
senses.example: That bony fellow could use a few hot dinners.

senses.definition: Having prominent bones.
senses.example: Her bony wrists and sharp elbows made her look much thinner than she was.

core.definition: Very thin, with bones that stick out under the skin, such as elbows, knees or a face.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a clear long 'ee'. Don't confuse it with 'bonny,' which is a different word.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. Calling someone bony can sound unkind, so it is usually used for body parts or in a descriptive way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'bony' to describe prominent bones, often of elbows, knees or faces. Calling a person bony can hurt their feelings, so 'thin' or 'slender' is kinder. The word is also used in biology, as in 'bony fish,' which is a formal term.

distinctions.note: Thin is neutral and polite; bony focuses on bones that show through the skin, which can sound harsh.
Gaunt is more negative and suggests illness, hunger or extreme weight loss.

examples.everyday: Her elbows looked bony after she lost so much weight, so her family asked if she was feeling okay.
examples.professional: The biology team's report on the bony fish specimens noted an unusually calcified spine.
examples.analytical: Vertebrate taxonomy distinguishes cartilaginous fishes from bony fishes, and that split rests on the composition of the skeleton.

nuance.analogy: Like a coat hanger under a thin shirt: the frame shows through the outer layer.
nuance.etymology: From bone plus the suffix -y, meaning 'having the quality of'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'bonny,' which means pretty or healthy-looking and is mainly Scottish.
Using it as a polite compliment for someone's figure, when it can sound unkind.
Writing 'boney', which is a common misspelling.

core.definition: A deuterocanonical book about Judith, a Jewish widow who saves her besieged town by killing the Assyrian general Holofernes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on JOO; the second syllable is a weak schwa and ends with the 'th' sound, not 'ee' or 't'. 'Of' reduces to 'uv'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and reverent; Judith is celebrated as a heroine, though the violence of her act is debated.
nuance.usage_note: Catholics and Orthodox Christians treat it as Scripture; most Americans outside those traditions know it little. Used mainly in church, seminary and literature or art classes.

distinctions.note: Both feature a heroine saving her people, but Esther is in the Hebrew canon and Judith is not.
Both are deuterocanonical narratives, but Tobit is a family story and Judith a military one.

examples.everyday: I saw a painting of Judith and Holofernes at the museum, and I finally read the Book of Judith.
examples.professional: In my seminary course we compared the Book of Judith with the story of Jael in Judges.
examples.analytical: The Book of Judith's historical inaccuracies, such as calling Nebuchadnezzar king of Assyria, suggest it is didactic fiction.

nuance.analogy: A tale of courage in which a seemingly powerless widow defeats an army.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yehudit, meaning 'Jewess' or 'woman of Judah'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'JOO-dith' with a hard 'd' stress on the end; the final sound is a weak 'th'.
Looking for it in a Protestant Bible; it is usually only in the Apocrypha.
Confusing Judith with Judas.
nuance.biblical_note: Judith (Hebrew Yehudit, 'Jewess') appears in the Apocrypha in the RSV, not the Protestant Old Testament. Judith 8 introduces her as a devout widow who rebukes the town leaders for testing God. Judith 13 narrates how she kills Holofernes in his tent. Judith 16 records her song of praise.

traditions.view: Judith is included in many Orthodox Bibles as Scripture, read with respect as part of the Old Testament.
Judith is a deuterocanonical book affirmed as canonical and inspired at the Council of Trent.
Protestants generally exclude Judith from the canon; Lutherans and Anglicans may read it as edifying but not as a source of doctrine.

senses.definition: In a boorish manner; uncultured.
senses.example: He laughed boorishly at the orchestra's quiet second movement.

core.definition: In a rude, crude or socially clumsy way, showing a lack of good manners or refinement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, BOOR. The -ish and -ly endings are unstressed, with a short i sound in -ish and a light -lee at the end. The r in boor is pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes behavior that is rude, clumsy or lacking refinement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use boorishly mainly in writing, reviews or formal criticism. In conversation, people usually say rudely, like a jerk or in a really rude way. Use boorishly when you want to emphasize crude, unrefined manners rather than simple rudeness.

distinctions.note: Rudely is everyday and general; boorishly emphasizes crude, unrefined behavior, a lack of social polish.
Coarsely describes rough or vulgar language or manners; boorishly describes a general pattern of clumsy rudeness.

examples.everyday: He talked over everyone at dinner and laughed at his own jokes, acting boorishly the whole night.
examples.professional: The vendor behaved boorishly during the negotiation, interrupting our team and refusing to listen.
examples.analytical: Kant would say that the man who speaks boorishly fails to respect the dignity of those he addresses.

nuance.analogy: Acting boorishly is like walking into a quiet room and turning on loud music without noticing anyone.
nuance.etymology: Formed from boor, meaning a crude person, with the adjective ending -ish and the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using boorishly for shy or quiet behavior; it means rude and crude, not reserved.
Stressing the second syllable; the stress belongs on BOOR, as in BOOR-ish-lee.

senses.definition: Suffering from boredom; mildly annoyed and restless through having nothing to do.
senses.example: He was feeling bored so he decided to play Minecraft.

senses.definition: Perforated by a hole or holes.

core.definition: Feeling tired and restless because you have nothing interesting to do or are not interested in what is happening.

pronunciation.tip: Say it like 'board,' with a clear American r and one syllable. Don't add an extra 'ed' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. Saying 'I'm bored' sounds like a complaint, so polite speakers choose their words more carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I'm bored in casual conversation, often as a complaint, such as 'I'm so bored, let's go out.' Saying it to a host, teacher or boss can sound rude, so use 'I'm not really into this' or 'I'm losing focus' instead. Bored with and bored of are both common in speech; bored by is less common.

distinctions.note: Bored describes how you feel, while boring describes what causes the feeling, as in 'the lecture was boring.'
Tired refers to physical exhaustion; bored refers to a lack of interest or stimulation.

examples.everyday: I'm bored, so do you want to grab a coffee?
examples.professional: Some people in the meeting looked bored during the budget review, so let's shorten the next slide.
examples.analytical: Heidegger treats boredom as a mood that reveals how we relate to time and meaning, not merely as a passing feeling.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone with no signal: it's switched on, but nothing is coming in.
common_mistakes: Saying I am boring when you mean I am bored; boring describes things, bored describes people.
Using bored for instead of bored with or bored of.

conversation.text: I'm so bored. Want to go see a movie?
The kids get bored on long car rides.
I got bored halfway through the book and stopped reading.

senses.definition: The capitalist class.
(historical) A class of citizens who were wealthier members of the third estate.
senses.example: Under the old monarchy, the bourgeoisie of Paris grew wealthy through trade and royal office.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: In Marxist theory, the class that owns the means of production; in general use, the middle class and its conventional values.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the last syllable, ZEE. Many learners say 'bor-zhwah-ZEE' or stress the first syllable, but Americans keep the boor sound and put the strongest stress on the end.

nuance.connotation: Often negative in political or critical writing, implying materialism or pretension, but neutral in sociology when describing a middle class.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bourgeoisie mostly in academic, political, or literary contexts, especially when discussing Marx or class. In everyday talk, people say middle class. Calling someone bourgeois is an insult implying conventional, materialistic tastes, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Middle class is the neutral term used in everyday American English, while bourgeoisie carries Marxist or critical overtones.
The proletariat is the working class that sells its labor, while the bourgeoisie owns capital in Marxist analysis.

examples.everyday: My neighbor jokes that the whole suburb is full of bourgeoisie, but he's just being sarcastic.
examples.professional: Our policy memo describes the middle-income target audience, though an academic reader might call them the bourgeoisie.
examples.analytical: Marx argued that the bourgeoisie, owning the means of production, held power over the proletariat in capitalist societies.

nuance.analogy: The bourgeoisie is like the owner of the factory in a story about labor: the one who owns the machines while others run them.
nuance.etymology: From French bourgeois, from Old French borjois, from Late Latin burgensis, meaning a town dweller, from burgus, a fortified town.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the stress by putting it on the first syllable.
Using bourgeoisie as an adjective, when the adjective is bourgeois.

bourgeoisie.etymology: from *bourgeois* (“a class of citizens who were wealthier members of the Third Estate”), from bourgeois, “burghers”, i.e. townspeople.

senses.definition: A swaggering show of defiance or courage.
senses.example: The angry customer stood in the middle of the showroom and voiced his complaints with loud bravado.

senses.definition: A superficial show of courage. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: His bravado in the poker game hid how nervous he really was.

core.definition: A show of confidence or boldness, often put on to impress others or to hide fear.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'VAH.' The first vowel is a reduced or short ah sound, and the final -o is pronounced like 'oh,' not 'ah.'

nuance.connotation: Often negative, suggesting the boldness is fake or excessive. It can be neutral or admiring when describing a performer's flair.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bravado in news, sports, and everyday talk to describe a showy attitude, such as 'He put on a lot of bravado before the game.' It is common in phrases like 'false bravado.' It is more than casual but not stiff, so it fits both conversation and writing.

distinctions.note: Bravery is real courage, while bravado is a show of courage that may not be real.
Swagger is a confident walk or manner, while bravado focuses on boasting or defiance, often covering fear.

collocations: put on a show of bravado

examples.everyday: He talked a big game about the marathon, but I think it was just bravado.
examples.professional: The team's bravado in the planning meeting made the risks sound smaller than they really were.
examples.analytical: Bravado often works as a defense mechanism, allowing speakers to project certainty while concealing anxiety.

nuance.analogy: Bravado is like a loud costume: it looks impressive from a distance, but it does not change what is underneath.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish bravada, 'boast' or 'display of bravery,' from bravo, 'brave.'
common_mistakes: Confusing bravado with bravery and using it as a compliment for real courage.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'BRAH-vah-doh.'

bravado.etymology: From French *bravade* (“bragging or boasting”), from Italian *bravata*, from verb *bravare* (“brag, boast”), from *bravo*.

senses.definition: A construction in or around a harbor designed to break the force of the sea and to provide shelter for vessels lying inside.
senses.example: Fishing boats rode out the storm safely behind the granite breakwater at the harbor entrance.

senses.definition: A wooden or concrete barrier, usually perpendicular to the shore, intended to prevent the movement of sand along a coast.
senses.example: The county built a timber breakwater along the beach to stop sand from washing away.

senses.definition: A low bulkhead across the forecastle deck of a ship which diverts water breaking over the bows into the scuppers.
senses.example: The crew inspected the forward breakwater to keep waves from pouring over the bow onto the deck.

core.definition: A wall or barrier built in the sea, at a harbor or along a shore, to block waves and protect boats or the beach.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on BRAYK, with a lighter secondary stress on the second syllable. The final syllable is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so say 'waw-ter' with a soft, flapped t that sounds like a d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical or descriptive term for coastal structures.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use breakwater for offshore walls of stone or concrete that protect harbors and marinas, and it appears in local news about storms, dredging and beach erosion. In everyday talk people often just say 'the jetty' or 'the wall out there' if they are talking about a harbor. It is not used for a wall on a beach; that is a seawall.

distinctions.note: A jetty extends from the shore into the water mainly to keep a river or harbor channel open, while a breakwater is a separate barrier that shelters a harbor from waves.
A seawall runs along the shoreline to hold back waves and erosion, while a breakwater stands offshore in the water.

examples.everyday: We walked out to the end of the breakwater to watch the sunset over the bay.
examples.professional: The county engineers want to repair the breakwater before the next hurricane season, since the storm damage has exposed the marina.
examples.analytical: The breakwater shows how a human structure can change the natural shape of a coastline, since the sand builds up on one side and erodes on the other.

nuance.analogy: A breakwater is like a hand held up in front of a candle: it does not stop the wind everywhere, but it protects the flame behind it.
nuance.etymology: Compound of break (to shatter or stop the force of) and water.
common_mistakes: Confusing breakwater with seawall, which is built along the shore rather than out in the water.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'wah-tur' with a hard t; in American speech the t is flapped and the vowel is often reduced.

senses.definition: The handle of a broom (sweeping tool); (sometimes) the entire broom.
A broom imbued with magic, enabling one to fly astride the handle.
senses.example: The old witch mounted her broomstick, cackled, and soared over the moonlit rooftops.

senses.definition: A control stick of an airplane or other vehicle.
senses.example: The pilot gripped the broomstick and eased it back to raise the nose of the plane.

senses.definition: (rare) A firearm.
senses.example: Keep that broomstick pointed at the ground, Earl, until we see what's in the brush.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To fly on a broomstick, as witches are said to.
senses.example: As a child, she dreamed of broomsticking over the rooftops like the witches in her storybooks.

core.definition: The long wooden handle of a broom, used for sweeping the floor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, broom, and give stick a lighter stress. Do not add a vowel between the m and the s; say 'broom-stik' cleanly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is an ordinary household object, and in fairy tales it is associated with witches.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use broomstick mostly for the handle of a broom, often when cleaning or in a funny phrase about witches flying. When Americans talk about a broom, they usually say 'broom', not 'broomstick', unless they mean the handle specifically. The word also appears in children's stories and Halloween jokes.

distinctions.note: A broom is the whole sweeping tool, while a broomstick is specifically the long handle.

examples.everyday: The broom head came off, so I'm just using the broomstick until I buy a new one.
examples.professional: Facilities asked us to check whether the broomstick was damaged before ordering new janitorial supplies.
examples.analytical: The witch's broomstick in folklore marks a boundary between domestic labor and forbidden flight, turning an ordinary tool into a symbol of transgression.

nuance.analogy: A broomstick is like the spine of a broom: the part you hold, while the bristles do the actual work.
nuance.etymology: From broom (Old English brōm) plus stick, the handle or stick.
common_mistakes: Saying 'broom stick' as two separate words in formal writing; 'broomstick' is one word.
Using broomstick for the broom head, which is the bristle part.

senses.definition: To inflict brutal violence on.
senses.example: The guards brutalized the prisoners during the riot, and the investigation later confirmed it.

senses.definition: To make brutal, cruel or harsh.
To live or behave like a brute.
senses.example: Years of working in that cutthroat office slowly brutalized him until he treated everyone like an enemy.

core.definition: To treat someone with extreme violence or cruelty, or to make a person or place coarse, harsh, or dehumanized.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the middle syllable as a weak 'tuh'. The ending '-ize' sounds like 'eyes', not 'eez'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes serious harm and is strong in tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use brutalize mainly in news, legal, and literary contexts about violence or abuse, such as 'brutalized by police' or 'brutalized prisoners'. It can also describe social or emotional damage, as in 'brutalized by poverty'. In casual speech, it sounds dramatic, so people often say 'beat up' or 'abuse' instead.

distinctions.note: Abuse is a broader word for mistreatment; brutalize specifically implies violent, harsh, or dehumanizing treatment.
Hurt is a general word for causing pain; brutalize suggests severe, often repeated, violence or harshness.

examples.everyday: The coach's endless punishment drills really brutalized the kids, and half of them quit.
examples.professional: Deep budget cuts brutalized the small team, and morale dropped sharply after the reorganization.
examples.analytical: Totalitarian regimes often brutalize ordinary citizens so that fear replaces trust and public life becomes silent.

nuance.analogy: To brutalize someone is like wearing down a stone with a hammer: each blow seems small, but the damage accumulates.
nuance.etymology: From brutal, with the verb-forming suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in 'brutal-IZE'; the first syllable carries the main stress.
Using brutalize only for physical violence; it can also describe emotional or social harm.

senses.definition: Full of bubbles.
senses.example: Whip the egg white into a bubbly froth.

senses.definition: Cheerful, lively.
senses.example: She has a bubbly personality.

senses.definition: Having the characteristics of bubbles.
senses.example: The architecture of the conservatory was bubbly.

senses.definition: Having the characteristics of economic bubbles.
senses.example: Analysts warned the bubbly housing market could collapse by next spring.

senses.definition: Champagne.
senses.example: We're getting married–this calls for a bottle of bubbly!

core.definition: Lively, cheerful and friendly, with an upbeat, talkative personality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BUB. Keep the l sound clear before the ee, and do not add an extra vowel between the b and the l.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests warmth and energy, though applied to a serious adult it can sound slightly childish.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bubbly to praise someone who is upbeat and friendly, such as a receptionist or a waiter. In a professional setting it is a compliment, but it can sound patronizing if used to dismiss an adult's serious ideas. As a noun, bubbly is casual slang for champagne or sparkling wine, as in 'Let's pop the bubbly'.

distinctions.note: Perky suggests brisk, chipper energy; bubbly suggests warm, effervescent happiness and talkativeness.
Effervescent is more formal and literary, and it describes lively enthusiasm; bubbly is the everyday American word.

examples.everyday: She's so bubbly, she makes everyone smile when they walk into the bakery.
examples.professional: Our new hire is bubbly in meetings, but she asks sharp questions that the senior engineers miss.
examples.analytical: Critics note that bubbly often works as a label for enthusiasm, rewarding surface cheer over substantive argument, especially when applied to women.

nuance.analogy: Like a glass of sparkling soda, lively and fizzing with energy.
nuance.etymology: From bubble with the suffix -y, meaning full of or like.
common_mistakes: Using bubbly for champagne in formal wine talk, where champagne or sparkling wine is the correct term.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long u, rather than the short u in 'bub'.

senses.definition: Insecticide in aerosol form for killing household pests.
senses.example: This can of bug spray says that it "kills most bugs in seconds" and that you should avoid getting any of it on yourself and should wash and launder thoroughly if that happens, although it is not poisonous to humans.

senses.definition: Insect repellent in aerosol form, such as one sprays on one's clothing and/or skin to keep away mosquitoes, gnats, flies, midges, etc.
senses.example: This can of bug spray says that it is nontoxic to humans and pets and that you should periodically reapply it to your arms and clothing as needed.

core.definition: A spray that keeps mosquitoes, flies, ticks and other biting insects away from your skin or clothes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SPRAY and say bug with a short u and a lighter secondary stress. The r in spray is pronounced, and the spr blends into one smooth cluster.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. You would buy it at a store or lend it to a friend before a hike.
nuance.usage_note: Bug spray is the everyday American term for insect repellent that you spray on your body or clothes. Brand names such as Off! and Cutter are common, and many Americans use the phrase even for repellents that are not pesticides. For insecticide to spray in a house, people say insect spray or pest spray. A natural request is 'Do you have any bug spray?' and the answer is 'Yes, here you go' or 'Sorry, I left mine at home.'

distinctions.note: Insect repellent is the more formal or technical term, often used on labels, while bug spray is the everyday phrase.
Insecticide kills insects and is used on plants and in houses, while bug spray usually repels insects from your skin and clothes.

examples.everyday: Did you bring bug spray? The mosquitoes are brutal down by the lake tonight.
examples.professional: Hand out bug spray and sunscreen to the field crew before the site survey.
examples.analytical: Bug spray works as a chemical barrier by interfering with insects' ability to detect and land on skin, not by killing them.

nuance.analogy: Bug spray is like a 'do not disturb' sign for mosquitoes: it does not stop them, but it makes you a less appealing target.
nuance.etymology: A compound of bug and spray, both long-established English words.
common_mistakes: Calling it bug killer for a repellent; a killer kills insects, while bug spray usually repels them.
Using a or an with it as if countable; say some bug spray or a can of bug spray.

conversation.text: Put on some bug spray, or the mosquitoes are going to eat you alive.
Did anybody bring bug spray? I'm getting eaten alive.
This bug spray smells awful, but it works.

senses.definition: To destroy by fire.
senses.example: The old church was burned out in the 1960s and never fully rebuilt.

senses.definition: To become extinguished due to lack of fuel.
senses.example: The candle finally burned out.

senses.definition: To become nonfunctional (especially of lightbulbs or similar light-producing devices).
senses.example: The porch light burned out, so we couldn't see the steps when we got home.

senses.definition: To tire due to overwork; to overwork to one's limit.
senses.example: After six months of twelve-hour workdays, most people just burn out and quit.

senses.definition: To cause (someone) to tire due to overwork; to cause (someone) to overwork to one's limit.
senses.example: After three double shifts, the nurse was completely burned out and needed a week off.

senses.definition: To end one's shift at a job.
senses.example: I start my shift at three in the afternoon, and get to burn out at midnight.

senses.definition: To have one's tires skid against the ground; to peel off, peel out.
senses.example: The sedan's rear tires burned out on the wet pavement as he spun the wheel.

senses.definition: To make (someone) unavailable for work involving exposure to ionizing radiation by employing (the person) in such work until the person's accumulated exposure reaches the maximum permitted for an administrative period, typically a year.
senses.example: The repairs on this nuclear reactor have burned out every welder in the province.

senses.definition: To use up too much energy when first bowled and to therefore not finish strongly.
senses.example: Our anchor bowler burned out in the second game and lost the match.

senses.definition: To be destroyed by fire.
senses.example: An abandoned tank was burning out at the edge of the battlefield.

core.definition: Exhausted and emotionally drained from long periods of stress, overwork, or demanding responsibilities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'out'. The '-ed' is pronounced as a /d/ sound, and the adjective form is often written 'burned-out' with a hyphen before a noun.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests long-term exhaustion and loss of motivation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'm burned out' in everyday talk about work, school, or caregiving. It is more common in American English than 'burnt out'. A natural reply is 'That's rough, maybe take a few days off.'

distinctions.note: Tired is usually temporary and physical. Burned out is longer-lasting and includes emotional exhaustion.
Exhausted is a general word for being very tired. Burned out implies a chronic loss of energy caused by pressure or responsibilities.
Fried is a very informal synonym that means worn out or overwhelmed. Burned out is more common in workplace and health contexts.

examples.everyday: I'm so burned out after the holidays that I just want to sit on the couch.
examples.professional: Several engineers on the platform team are burned out, so we need to rebalance the on-call rotation.
examples.analytical: Burned-out workers often describe a loss of meaning rather than mere fatigue, which is why the term names a depletion of the self.

nuance.analogy: Like a candle that has used up all its wax and now gives off only a faint glow.
