nuance.usage_note: Americans use coexist in everyday talk about people, animals, ideas and politics, such as 'Can these two approaches coexist?' In casual conversation people often say get along or live with, which sound warmer. Note that coexist already means together, so 'coexist together' is redundant, though you will hear it.

distinctions.note: Live together usually means sharing a home, often as a couple or roommates, while coexist means existing in the same place or time without necessarily sharing a home.
Get along is casual and focuses on friendly relations; coexist is more neutral and says nothing about warmth, only that both continue to exist.
Cohabit is formal and usually refers to an unmarried couple living together; coexist has no such implication.

examples.everyday: Our two cats have finally learned to coexist in the same apartment, although they still don't share a bed.
examples.professional: We designed the new service so the legacy API and the new one can coexist during the migration.
examples.analytical: Many philosophers argue that libertarian free will and strict determinism cannot coexist, while compatibilists deny this.

nuance.analogy: Like two radio stations broadcasting on different frequencies in the same city, each present without drowning out the other.
nuance.etymology: From Latin co- (together) plus exist, from existere, to come forth or stand forth.
common_mistakes: Saying coexist together, which is redundant in standard American English.
Placing stress on co- rather than on ZIST.
Using coexist with a noun object without a preposition, as in coexist the two systems instead of coexist with the other system.

senses.definition: A form of reasoning where the truth or falsehood of a belief is defined by its coherence with the rest of the believer's knowledge and experiences.

core.definition: An epistemological theory that a belief is justified when it fits coherently with the believer's other beliefs and experiences, not because it rests on a foundation.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the middle syllable, 'HEER,' and the 'ent' reduces to 'un.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it is used in philosophy classrooms and research writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coherentism mainly in epistemology courses and philosophy of science discussions. It is usually contrasted with foundationalism, the view that beliefs must rest on basic, self-evident truths. In everyday speech, people say 'fits with everything else I know' rather than using the technical term.

distinctions.note: Foundationalism holds that justified beliefs rest on basic beliefs that need no further support, while coherentism says justification comes from mutual fit among beliefs.
Coherence is the quality of fitting together logically, while coherentism is a theory about how that quality produces justification.

examples.everyday: My dad says he only believes something if it fits with everything else he knows, which I guess is a kind of coherentism.
examples.professional: In the research memo, we treated our findings as a web of evidence and used coherentism to check which results support each other.
examples.analytical: On coherentism, a belief is justified not by a foundation of self-evident truths but by its place in a mutually supporting system of beliefs.

nuance.analogy: Coherentism is like a jigsaw puzzle: each piece is justified by how well it fits with the others, not by a single piece that holds everything up.
nuance.etymology: From coherent (from Latin cohaerere, 'to stick together') plus -ism.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle vowel as in 'hair,' which is not the standard American form; say 'HEER.'
Confusing coherentism with coherency, which is a related noun but not the name of the theory.
Using coherentism to mean 'consistency' in general; the term names a specific theory of justification.

senses.definition: Of or supporting coherentism.
senses.example: Her coherentist approach to justification made sense of the whole argument, though her colleagues remained skeptical.

senses.definition: One who supports coherentism in terms of truth or justification.
senses.example: As a coherentist, Mark argued that a belief is justified when it fits well with his other beliefs.

core.definition: A person who holds that beliefs are justified by how well they fit together; also describes this view or someone who holds it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HEER, the second syllable, as in coherent, and the middle syllable is a reduced vowel. Americans pronounce the r clearly, and the final -ist is short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical label for a position in philosophy, used neither as praise nor as criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word almost only in philosophy, especially epistemology, where it is contrasted with foundationalism. The noun names a person and the adjective names the view, as in 'a coherentist account of justification'. Outside academic circles, you would simply say someone thinks their beliefs must hang together.

distinctions.note: A foundationalist holds that some beliefs are justified directly, without needing support from other beliefs; a coherentist grounds justification in mutual support among beliefs.
That theory says what makes a belief true is its fit with other beliefs, while coherentism about justification concerns what makes a belief reasonable to hold; the two are related but distinct.

examples.everyday: At dinner, my roommate said he's kind of a coherentist: if a new idea doesn't fit what he already believes, he doesn't trust it.
examples.professional: In our reading group, the coherentist position came up again, since the paper argues that justification depends on how beliefs fit together.
examples.analytical: A coherentist must explain why a set of mutually supporting beliefs is not merely a closed circle of assumptions that could all be false.

nuance.analogy: A coherentist's beliefs are like the pieces of a jigsaw: each is justified by how well it locks with the others.
nuance.etymology: From coherent, from Latin cohaerere 'to stick together', plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Confusing coherentist, a term for a view or person in philosophy, with coherent, which means logically consistent or clear, in everyday conversation.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in koh-HAIR-entist; the stress is on HEER.

senses.definition: An undertaker.
senses.example: In the 1950s novel, the cold cook arrived at the farmhouse before the sun rose.

core.definition: A kitchen worker who prepares cold dishes such as salads, cold appetizers and sliced meats.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on COOK, the second word, and the l in cold is clear before the d. Say cook with the short oo of 'book', not the long oo of 'boot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a plain job title in restaurant kitchens.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this mainly in restaurant and catering kitchens, where the cold station is often called garde manger. The undertaker sense in some dictionaries is rare and dated, and Americans would say funeral director instead, so avoid it. A natural sentence is 'Our cold cook makes all the salads.'

distinctions.note: A hot cook works at the stove or grill and makes food served hot.
Some dictionaries list this sense, but it is rare and dated; in the US say funeral director.

examples.everyday: My cousin works as a cold cook at a seafood place, so she makes all the salads.
examples.professional: Can you ask the cold cook to plate the appetizers before the main courses go out?
examples.analytical: In a professional kitchen the cold cook's station is kept apart from the hot line to prevent cross-contamination.

nuance.analogy: Like the chef who only works the salad bowl while others handle the stove.
nuance.etymology: Cold from Old English ceald; cook from Old English cōc, from Latin coquus.
common_mistakes: Using cold cook for an undertaker, a dated slang sense most Americans won't recognize
Pronouncing cook with the long oo of 'boot'

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, caused by, or partaking in combustion.

core.definition: Relating to, caused by, or involved in combustion, the process of burning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the first syllable is a reduced schwa, not the 'comb' of combing hair. The ending is -iv, rhyming with 'give,' not 'five.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a process without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adjective outside chemistry, engineering, and technical writing. In everyday talk they say 'combustion' or 'combustible' instead. 'Combustible' means something that can catch fire easily, while 'combustive' describes the process of burning itself.

distinctions.note: Combustible describes a material able to catch fire easily, while combustive describes what relates to or results from the burning process.
Flammable is the everyday safety word for things that catch fire easily, so Americans use it on warning labels, while combustive is a technical adjective.

examples.everyday: My mechanic said the car's combustive problem comes from a dirty fuel injector.
examples.professional: The engineering team reviewed the combustive performance of the new turbine under high-pressure tests.
examples.analytical: Read as a combustive image, the forge in Malachi becomes a figure for purification, where what is impure is burned away.

nuance.analogy: A combustive process is like a candle flame: the wax gives off fuel, and the flame is the burning itself.
nuance.etymology: From Latin combustus, past participle of comburere, 'to burn up,' from com- (together) and urere (to burn).
common_mistakes: Using 'combustive' for things that burn easily; that meaning belongs to 'combustible.'
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'KOM-bus-tiv.'

senses.definition: To emerge or become known, especially unexpectedly.
senses.example: Unless anything comes up, I'll be there every day this week.

senses.definition: To happen or occur.
senses.example: His shift came up, so he had to go to work.

senses.definition: To approach a time or scheduled event.
senses.example: We're coming up on the interview in the last half-hour of the program.

senses.definition: To come towards; to approach.
senses.example: I was standing on the corner when Nick came up and asked for a cigarette.

senses.definition: To be revealed to have a certain value, quality, or status.
senses.example: The movie didn't come up to our expectations.

senses.definition: To come to attention and present oneself; to arrive or appear.
senses.example: At some point in the conversation my name came up, and I readily agreed to their proposition.

senses.definition: To appear (before a judge or court).
senses.example: He came up before a judge and was fined a thousand dollars.

senses.definition: To draw near in time.
senses.example: The summer holidays are coming up.

senses.definition: To reach in height.
senses.example: You have to come up to here to ride this roller-coaster.

senses.definition: To rise (above the horizon).
senses.example: It'll be warmer once the sun comes up.

senses.definition: To grow up; to experience a childhood.
senses.example: I came up in Baltimore.

senses.definition: To do well or be successful.
senses.example: Watch out for him, he's been coming up lately.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see come,‎ up.
senses.example: I came up the ladder carefully, holding the bucket in my right hand.

senses.definition: An opportunity.
senses.example: This promotion is a real come up, and I'm not letting it slip by.

core.definition: To be raised or mentioned in conversation, or to happen unexpectedly. Also, to approach a scheduled time or event.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrasal verb the stress falls on UP, not COME, so say 'kum-UP'. Learners often stress COME, which sounds unnatural to Americans.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe something pleasant or unpleasant, depending on what came up.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'come up' constantly to say that a topic was raised, as in 'It came up in the meeting', or that something unexpected happened, as in 'Something came up, so I can't make it.' It is intransitive, so you do not put an object after it: say 'The topic came up', not 'came up the topic'. The reply 'Oh, okay' or 'Let me know' is typical.
word_family: come-up (noun, an opportunity or a rise in status)

distinctions.note: Bring up is transitive and requires an object, as in 'I brought up the budget', while come up is intransitive and describes a topic arising on its own.
Arise is more formal and written, often used in reports, while come up is the everyday spoken choice.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I can't make dinner tonight because something came up at work.
examples.professional: The security question came up during the sprint review, so we added it to next week's agenda.
examples.analytical: The problem of other minds comes up whenever philosophers try to justify belief in mental states.

nuance.analogy: Like a fish surfacing in a lake, appearing without warning from below.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cuman 'to come' and 'up', a direction meaning toward a higher point or into view.
common_mistakes: Using a direct object, as in 'I came up the topic'; say 'I brought up the topic'.
Confusing 'come up' with 'come up with', which means to produce an idea.

conversation.text: Your name came up in the meeting today.
Something came up at work, so I can't make it tonight.
A guy came up to me and asked for directions.
My birthday is coming up next week.

related: come-up (noun, an opportunity or a rise in status)

senses.definition: Operations performed by a compiler (the “compile-time operations”).
senses.example: Compile-time checks caught the mismatched types before the program ever ran.

senses.definition: Programming language requirements that must be met by source code for it to be successfully compiled (the “compile-time requirements”).
senses.example: The compile-time rules require every variable to be declared before its first use.

senses.definition: Properties of the program that can be reasoned about during compilation.
senses.example: Because the array size is a compile-time constant, the compiler can reserve memory upfront.

core.definition: Happening or applied while source code is being translated into executable form, before the program runs.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on time, the final word, and compile keeps a lighter secondary stress. In fast speech the first word may reduce, so clearly say the final time.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is plain technical language that engineers use without emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Programmers use compile-time in code reviews, documentation, and language specifications. Americans on engineering teams say it casually as an ordinary term. Outside software it sounds like jargon. The opposite is run-time, or runtime.

distinctions.note: Run-time happens while the program executes; compile-time happens earlier, when the compiler translates the code.
Static often means checked before execution; compile-time checks are one kind of static analysis, which is a broader term.

examples.everyday: Our build failed at compile time, so the app never even ran on my phone.
examples.professional: Let's add a compile-time check so the team catches the missing field before it reaches production.
examples.analytical: A language with strong compile-time guarantees shifts many failures from runtime to the moment the code is translated.

nuance.analogy: Like proofreading a manuscript before it goes to the printer, rather than after readers find the typos.
nuance.etymology: Compile from Latin compilare; time from Old English tima.
common_mistakes: Writing compile time without a hyphen when it modifies a noun, as in a compile time error.
Saying at the compile-time instead of at compile time; the phrase takes no article.

senses.definition: Not convex; having at least one internal angle greater than 180 degrees.
senses.example: The hull of the kayak has a concave section that makes it harder to flip.

senses.definition: Satisfying the property that all segments connecting two points on the function's graph lie below the function.
senses.example: If the function is concave, every line segment between two points on its graph lies below the curve.

senses.definition: Curved like the inner surface of a sphere or bowl.
Hollow; empty.
senses.example: The concave shell of the old cypress stump was home to a family of raccoons.

senses.definition: A concave surface or curve.
senses.example: She ran her palm over the concave of the spoon's bowl, checking for dents.

senses.definition: The vault of the sky.
senses.example: The psalmist praised God for stretching out the concave of heaven like a tent.

senses.definition: One of the celestial spheres of the Ptolemaic or geocentric model of the world.
senses.example: Aristotle makes [Fire] to move to the concave of the Moon. - Thomas Salusbury (1661).

senses.definition: An element of a curved grid used to separate desirable material from tailings or chaff in mining and harvesting.
senses.example: The mill's curved concave screen separates the valuable ore from the worthless tailings.

senses.definition: An indentation running along the base of a surfboard, intended to increase lift.
senses.example: The surfer added a double concave to the deck for extra lift on steep waves.

senses.definition: An indented area on the top of a skateboard, providing a position for foot placement and increasing board strength.
senses.example: Her new skateboard has a deep concave that holds her feet in place during tricks.

senses.definition: A playing card made concave for use in cheating.
senses.example: The dealer slid a concave card from his sleeve and the table went quiet.

senses.definition: To render concave, or increase the degree of concavity.
senses.example: The machinist concaved the metal plate slightly so the bolts would seat flush.

core.definition: Curved inward, like the inside of a bowl or a cave; the opposite of convex, which curves outward.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the first vowel sounds like the 'o' in 'cot'. The second syllable rhymes with 'cave', not 'conk'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a plain descriptive word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use concave in math, science, design and everyday descriptions of shapes, such as a concave spoon or a concave mirror. In casual talk you might say 'curved in' or 'hollow', but concave is the precise word. A natural comment is 'That lens is concave, so it spreads light out.'

distinctions.note: Hollow means empty inside, while concave describes a surface that curves inward, even if the object is solid.
Convex is the opposite, describing a surface that bulges outward, like the outside of a ball.

examples.everyday: The back of this spoon is concave, so it holds a little soup without spilling.
examples.professional: Use a concave mirror in the test rig so the light focuses on the sensor.
examples.analytical: A function that is concave down has a graph that lies entirely below its tangent lines, which is the property we need for the proof.

nuance.analogy: A concave surface is like the inside of a bowl, where the edges curve up around a low center.
nuance.etymology: From Latin concavus, 'hollow, arched', from com- and cavus, 'hollow'.
common_mistakes: Confusing concave with convex, especially for lenses and mirrors.
Using concave to describe a person's body or a sound when hollow or sunken is the natural word.

concave.etymology: From Middle English *concave*, from Old French *concave*, from Latin *concavus*.

senses.definition: That can be condoned.
senses.example: Her friend's rudeness at dinner seemed condonable, since everyone knew he had been under enormous stress.

core.definition: Able to be forgiven or overlooked; not serious enough to need punishment, or excusable in the circumstances.

pronunciation.tip: The stress moves to the first syllable, unlike the verb 'condone', which is stressed on 'DONE'. The middle syllable is a short, reduced 'duh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It implies that something wrong is still wrong but can be overlooked.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'condonable' mostly in ethics, law, journalism and academic writing. In speech people more often say 'forgivable', 'excusable' or 'understandable'. Use it to describe something minor that you choose not to punish, not something serious.

distinctions.note: Forgivable describes a wrong that deserves forgiveness, while condonable suggests it can be overlooked without full forgiveness.
Excusable focuses on reasons or circumstances that reduce blame, while condonable focuses on whether it is acceptable to overlook the act.
Pardonable is more everyday and often used for small mistakes, while condonable has a more formal, moral tone.

examples.everyday: Showing up late once is condonable, but if you do it again we'll have a problem.
examples.professional: A one-time data entry error is condonable, but repeated mistakes in the audit trail are not, and they need a corrective plan.
examples.analytical: Whether a lie told to protect a friend is condonable depends on whether the harm it prevents outweighs the damage to trust.

nuance.analogy: Like a small scratch on a car that you decide to ignore: noticeable, but not worth stopping for.
nuance.etymology: From condone plus -able; condone comes from Latin condonare, 'to give up, pardon'.
common_mistakes: Using 'condonable' to mean 'able to condone', as in 'a condonable person'; the word describes an act that may be overlooked, not a person who overlooks.
Stressing the second syllable as in the verb, 'kun-DOHN-uh-bul', instead of the first syllable of the adjective.

senses.definition: An act of confirmation.

core.definition: The act of confirming something, such as checking that a booking, order, or fact is correct.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FER. The ending -ing is a short nasal sound, 'ming', not a long 'eeng' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a process without judging it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always say confirmation for the noun, as in 'Did you get the confirmation?' The noun confirming appears mainly in formal or technical writing about processes. In casual speech, people would say 'checking' or 'confirming it with them' as a verb.

distinctions.note: Confirmation is the normal noun for the result, such as a confirmation email; confirming is the process itself and is rarely used alone.
Verification means formal checking against evidence; confirming can be a lighter, informal act.

examples.everyday: Confirming the table by phone first kept us from waiting at the door on a busy Friday.
examples.professional: Confirming each order against the warehouse log is the step we keep skipping under deadline pressure.
examples.analytical: Confirming a theory with a single favorable observation is the kind of inference philosophers of science warn against.

nuance.analogy: Like checking your ticket at the gate: a quick look that turns a booking into a fact.
nuance.etymology: From confirm, from Latin confirmare 'to make firm'.
common_mistakes: Using confirming as the everyday noun where Americans say 'confirmation'.
Stretching the -ing ending into a long vowel; it is short, 'kun-FER-ming'.

senses.definition: The act or process of confiscating.
senses.example: The customs officers ordered the confiscation of the undeclared cash at the airport.

core.definition: The seizing of someone's property by an authority, such as the government or police, usually as a penalty.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SKAY, the syllable before -shun. The middle syllables reduce to 'fuh', not 'fye'. The ending sounds like 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative for the owner, since it means losing something taken by authority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use confiscation in news and legal contexts, such as 'federal confiscation of assets' or 'customs confiscation of fruit at the airport'. In casual talk, people often say 'took away' or 'took'. Using confiscation for a teacher taking a phone is a bit formal but understood.

distinctions.note: Seizure is the broader term for taking property by force or authority, including police seizing evidence; confiscation is a formal, often permanent taking, usually as a penalty.
Forfeiture is losing property because of a legal violation, often a crime; confiscation is the act of taking, and the two often overlap.
Expropriation is the government taking private property for public use, usually with compensation; confiscation usually means taking without compensation.

examples.everyday: After the confiscation of his phone in class, my son spent the whole dinner complaining.
examples.professional: The confiscation of the warehouse inventory by federal agents halted production for three weeks.
examples.analytical: Many political theorists treat the confiscation of property without consent as a basic violation of the social contract.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee taking the ball from a player who broke the rules and keeping it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin confiscare, 'to put into the public treasury', from com- 'together' and fiscus 'treasury, public purse'.
common_mistakes: Confusing confiscation with confirmation in spelling and sound.
Using confiscation for everyday taking; in casual speech Americans say 'took away'.

senses.definition: A large fire extending to many objects, or over a large space; a general burning.
senses.example: It took sixty firefighters to put out the conflagration.

senses.definition: A large-scale conflict.
senses.example: The border dispute threatened to ignite a regional conflagration involving three neighboring nations.

senses.definition: A situation of great passion or emotion.
senses.example: Their stormy romance was a conflagration of jealousy, longing, and passion that consumed everyone around them.

core.definition: A large, destructive fire that spreads across many buildings or a wide area, such as a wildfire or city blaze.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on GRAY, with a lighter stress on the first syllable, and the middle syllables flow as 'fluh.' Americans reduce 'fluh' to a quick schwa, and the g is hard before the r.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; it describes catastrophe, destruction, or uncontrolled spread.
nuance.usage_note: In American news, conflagration appears in headlines about wildfires and large building fires, but everyday speakers usually say 'big fire,' 'wildfire,' or 'the fire got out of control.' Using it in casual talk sounds dramatic, which can work for humor. Figurative uses, like 'a conflagration of protests,' are common in editorials.

distinctions.note: Fire is the everyday, neutral word. Conflagration names a large, destructive fire, usually spreading widely.
A blaze is a bright, active fire, often in a single house or building. A conflagration is larger and more destructive, spreading over an area.
Inferno is dramatic and often used figuratively for a terrible scene. Conflagration is more formal and suits news and reports better.

examples.everyday: My cousin's garage turned into a conflagration before the fire trucks even got there.
examples.professional: The data center fire became a conflagration that took down the backup servers for two days.
examples.analytical: Thucydides presents the civil strife at Corcyra as a moral conflagration that spread from city to city, consuming ordinary restraint.

nuance.analogy: Like a spark in dry grass: small at first, then a fire no one can contain.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conflagratio, from conflagrare 'to burn up completely', from com- 'together' + flagrare 'to burn'.
common_mistakes: Confusing conflagration with conflation, which means blending things together; the words look and sound similar.
Using conflagration for a candle or a small kitchen fire; the word is too strong for minor fires.

conflagration.etymology: From Middle French, from Latin *cōnflagrātiō* (“burning, conflagration”).

senses.definition: A sound that results from the passage of air through restrictions of the oral cavity; any sound that is not the nucleus of a syllable, the nucleus generally being a vowel.
A letter representing the sound of a consonant.
Consistent, harmonious, compatible, or in agreement.
Having the same sound.
Of or relating to consonants; made up of, or containing many, consonants.
Harmonizing together; accordant.
senses.example: consonant tones; consonant chords

core.definition: A speech sound made by blocking or narrowing the airflow in the mouth, such as the sounds of b, t, or s, as opposed to a vowel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle vowels reduce to a soft 'uh'. The word has three syllables, and the ending sounds like 'unt', not 'ent'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a standard term used in teaching, linguistics, and speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans learn this word early in school with 'vowels and consonants' and 'consonant blends' such as 'bl' or 'str'. In everyday speech it mostly appears when talking about spelling, reading, or pronunciation. It is used in the same way in British and American English.

distinctions.note: A vowel is a sound made with an open vocal tract, like the 'a' in 'cat', while consonants involve some blocking or narrowing of airflow.
Consonance means harmony or agreement, while a consonant is a speech sound; the two words look alike but have different meanings.

examples.everyday: The word 'strengths' ends in a tough cluster of consonants, so it is hard to say quickly.
examples.professional: Our speech recognition model still struggles with voiceless consonants in noisy audio.
examples.analytical: The phonological rule deletes a final consonant whenever another consonant comes before it.

nuance.analogy: Think of vowels as open sound and consonants as the lips, teeth, and tongue that shape it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consonans 'sounding together', from consonare; a consonant is sounded together with a vowel.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'consonant' (a speech sound) with 'consonance' (harmony) because the spellings look similar.
Pronouncing the last syllable as 'ent' (KON-suh-nent) instead of the reduced 'unt'.

consonant.etymology: From Middle English *consonant* or *consonaunt*, from Old French *consonant*, from Latin *cōnsonāns* (“sounding with”), from the prefix *con-* (“with”) + the present participle *sonāns* (“sounding”), from *sonāre* (“to sound”).

senses.definition: A stretch of road where work is being done; speed limits are lower and fines higher.

core.definition: A section of road where work is underway, usually with lower speed limits, lane closures, and higher fines for speeding.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on ZONE, and the second word gets the heavier beat. Say the -tion ending as 'shun' with a reduced vowel, and keep the r in construction.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but drivers often feel irritated by them. The sign itself is a warning, not an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase constantly on highways and city streets, in traffic reports, and in everyday talk about commuting. Road crews often say 'work zone' on signs, and 'construction zone' is the spoken equivalent. A natural reply to 'Traffic's terrible' is 'Yeah, there's a construction zone on the interstate.'

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning; 'work zone' is the more official term on government road signs, while 'construction zone' is the everyday phrase people use in conversation.
'Road work' names the activity itself, while 'construction zone' names the area where it happens.

collocations: slow down in a construction zone

examples.everyday: Slow down, there's a construction zone up ahead.
examples.professional: Our crew can't start the install until the Route 9 construction zone closes.
examples.analytical: A construction zone changes the legal duty of drivers, so the lower limit is a reasoned safety measure rather than a revenue tactic.

nuance.analogy: A construction zone is like a narrow hallway in a busy office where everyone must slow down while workers are moving equipment.
nuance.etymology: Construction comes from Latin construere, 'to pile together'; zone comes from Greek zone, 'belt'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'construction road' or 'work road' when Americans say 'construction zone'.
Stressing 'construction' on the second syllable (kun-STRUK-shun) instead of the third, the -tion sound is a reduced 'shun'.

conversation.text: Fines double in a construction zone, so slow down.
The speed limit drops to forty-five in the construction zone.
We crawled through a five-mile construction zone on the interstate.

senses.definition: The actual, substantial presence of the body of Christ with the bread and wine of the sacrament of the Lord's Supper; impanation, as opposed to transubstantiation.
An identity or union of substance.
senses.example: Lutherans teach consubstantiation, holding that Christ's body and blood are truly present with the bread and wine.

core.definition: The doctrine that Christ's body and blood are present together with the bread and wine in the Lord's Supper, without replacing them.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress is on 'AY', near the end, with secondary stress on 'kahn' and 'stan'. The 'ti' is pronounced 'shee', so the middle is 'stan-shee-AY'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in itself, but the term is often used by critics, and many Lutherans reject it as inaccurate for their view.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialist theological term, used in discussions of the Eucharist and the Reformation. Lutherans usually do not accept it as a label for their teaching, preferring 'sacramental union' or 'real presence'. Use it carefully, noting it is often an outsider's term.

distinctions.note: In transubstantiation the substance of bread and wine is changed into Christ's body and blood; in consubstantiation, as often described, both coexist.
Real presence is the broader belief that Christ is truly present in the sacrament, without explaining the mechanism.
Consubstantial describes being of the same substance, as in the Nicene Creed's statement about the Son and the Father.

examples.everyday: My Lutheran friend told me they don't actually call their view consubstantiation.
examples.professional: In seminary, I wrote a paper contrasting transubstantiation with what is often labeled consubstantiation.
examples.analytical: Luther rejected transubstantiation yet insisted on Christ's real presence, a position later critics labeled consubstantiation.

nuance.analogy: Think of fire in an iron rod: the iron stays iron and the fire is truly present in it, as an old illustration for this idea.
nuance.etymology: From Latin com- 'with' + substantia, 'substance', plus -ation; coined in the medieval period to describe coexistence of substances.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with transubstantiation, which means change of substance.
Misplacing stress on the first syllable.
Assuming it is the official Lutheran term.
nuance.biblical_note: The doctrine rests on Jesus' words at the Last Supper, 'This is my body' (Matthew 26:26-28; Mark 14:22-24; Luke 22:19-20). Paul in 1 Corinthians 10:16 says the cup and the bread are a participation in Christ's blood and body. 1 Corinthians 11:23-29 repeats the institution and warns against taking the Supper unworthily.

traditions.view: Catholics reject consubstantiation and teach transubstantiation: the substance of bread and wine changes into Christ's body and blood, while the appearances remain.
Orthodoxy teaches that the bread and wine truly become Christ's Body and Blood, and treats it as a mystery, without adopting scholastic terms such as transubstantiation or consubstantiation.

Lutherans teach the real presence 'in, with, and under' the bread and wine, and usually reject the label 'consubstantiation'. Reformed Christians hold a spiritual presence, and Baptists and many others see the Supper as a memorial.

senses.definition: The act of touching physically; being in close association.
The establishment of communication (with).
senses.example: I haven't been in contact with her for years.

senses.definition: The situation of being within sight of something; visual contact.
senses.example: The hikers lost visual contact with their guide in the thick fog.

senses.definition: A nodule designed to connect a device with something else.
senses.example: Touch the contact to ground and read the number again.

senses.definition: Someone who can be contacted, or with whom one is in communication.
senses.example: Who is the company's contact for sales queries?

senses.definition: A means of communication with a person, especially in the form of a telephone number.
senses.example: Please leave your contact with the front desk so we can reach you.

senses.definition: A contact lens.
senses.example: She put in her contacts before the morning meeting.

senses.definition: A device designed for repetitive connections.
senses.example: The relay's contact wore out after a million switching cycles.

senses.definition: Contact juggling.
senses.example: I bought myself a new contact ball last week

senses.definition: The plane between two adjacent bodies of dissimilar rock.
senses.example: The geologist mapped the contact between the granite and the surrounding limestone.

senses.definition: To touch; to come into physical contact with.
senses.example: The side of the car contacted the pedestrian.

senses.definition: To establish communication with (something or someone).
senses.example: I am trying to contact my sister.

core.definition: Communication or close association with someone, or the state of being in touch with them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KON. The first vowel is the American open o from the cot-caught merger, and the final t is often unreleased or lightly pronounced, not a strong puff of air.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive when describing a helpful relationship and negative when describing an unwanted or dangerous exposure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say get in contact with or stay in contact with someone, and in business they often ask for a contact, meaning a person to call. As a verb, contact is common in email and phone talk: Please contact me tomorrow. People also say be in touch in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Communication is the act or process of exchanging information; contact is the connection or channel through which it happens.
Connection can mean a personal bond or a link; contact is more specific to reaching or being reached by someone.

examples.everyday: Have you been in contact with your sister since she moved to Denver?
examples.professional: Please send me a contact for the vendor's account manager so I can follow up on the invoice.
examples.analytical: Prolonged contact between different communities changed both their religious practices and their moral vocabulary.

nuance.analogy: Contact is like a phone line: it is the connection that lets a message pass in either direction.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contactus, meaning a touching, from contingere, to touch.
common_mistakes: Using contact to with the meaning reach out to; in American English it is usually contact or get in touch with someone.
Saying contact me to a number; say call me or contact me at, followed by the email or phone number.

contact.etymology: From Latin *contactus*, from *contingō* (“to touch on all sides”), from *tangō* (“to touch”).

senses.definition: From the same time period, coexistent in time; contemporaneous.
senses.example: Medieval theologian Thomas Aquinas and his contemporary Bonaventure both taught in Paris.

senses.definition: Modern, of the present age (shorthand for ‘contemporary with the present’).
Someone or something belonging to the same time period (as someone or something else)
senses.example: Cervantes was a contemporary of Shakespeare.

senses.definition: Something existing at the same time.
senses.example: Bonaventure was a contemporary of Aquinas, and their debates shaped later scholastic thought.

senses.definition: (dated) A rival newspaper or magazine.
senses.example: The editor fumed that the rival contemporary had scooped the story again.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Modern and belonging to the present day; also, existing or happening at the same time as something else.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on TEM, and the second r-colored syllable is weak, so 'rair' is quick. Many learners stress the last syllable or say a full 'ar' vowel in the middle; keep the middle reduced and end with a light 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests being up to date and relevant, but in a historical context it simply means 'from the same time'.
nuance.usage_note: In American speech, contemporary often describes style, such as contemporary furniture, contemporary music, or contemporary issues. Modern can mean the early twentieth century onward in art history, so use contemporary when you mean 'current' or 'today's'. Americans also use it for religious music, as in 'contemporary worship'.

distinctions.note: Modern can mean recent or from the early 1900s onward, and it can sound more neutral; contemporary specifically means of the present time.
Current stresses what is happening right now; contemporary also emphasizes belonging to the same period as something else.
Contemporaneous is more formal and technical and means existing at the same time; contemporary is the common everyday word.

examples.everyday: I really like contemporary jazz, the newer stuff that still has real melody and doesn't sound like a copy of the old records.
examples.professional: Our contemporary approach to model monitoring tracks drift in real time, so we catch problems before customers notice them.
examples.analytical: Contemporary theologians often struggle to reconcile evolutionary biology with traditional teaching about Adam, and their proposals vary widely.

nuance.analogy: Contemporary is like a shared calendar: everything written on the same page happens at the same time, and today's news is always on the current page.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin contemporarius, from Latin con- 'together' and tempus 'time'.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the word with five clear, full syllables instead of four with reduced vowels.
Using contemporary as a noun without a plural, saying 'a contemporary' when you mean one person from the same period, which is acceptable, but 'contemporaries' is the usual plural.

contemporary.etymology: From Medieval Latin *contemporārius*, from Latin *con-* (“with, together”) + *temporārius*, an adjective derived from *tempus* (“time”).

senses.definition: A trait of evolution in which species independently develop similar properties.

core.definition: The process by which unrelated species independently develop similar traits because they face similar environmental pressures.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VUR in convergent and on LOO in evolution. The -ent and -ion endings are weak, so the vowels reduce to uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a scientific term that describes a pattern without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in biology classes, science journalism, and research papers. It is common in discussions of animals with similar shapes or abilities, such as dolphins and sharks. Non-scientists may say 'similar solutions evolved separately' to explain the same idea.

distinctions.note: Divergent evolution describes related species becoming different, while convergent evolution describes unrelated species becoming similar.
Homologous structures share ancestry, such as a human arm and a bat wing, while convergent traits arise separately, such as bird and bat wings.

collocations: a clear case of convergent evolution

examples.everyday: Did you know dolphins and sharks look alike because of convergent evolution?
examples.professional: In our genomics analysis, the similar protein structures suggest convergent evolution rather than shared ancestry.
examples.analytical: Convergent evolution shows that natural selection can produce similar solutions in unrelated lineages without a common ancestor.

nuance.analogy: Like two different people independently designing the same kind of tool because they faced the same problem.
nuance.etymology: Combines convergent, from Latin convergere ('to incline together'), with evolution, from Latin evolutio ('an unrolling').
common_mistakes: Thinking it means that species are closely related; the term describes similarity from separate origins.
Confusing it with convergence in ordinary joining, since the scientific sense is specific to evolution.

senses.definition: The act of correcting.
senses.example: The correction of the bug took only an hour once the team found the faulty loop.

senses.definition: A substitution for an error or mistake.
senses.example: The teacher marked the wrong answer and wrote a correction in red ink above it.

senses.definition: Punishment that is intended to rehabilitate an offender.
senses.example: The judge sentenced him to two years in a juvenile correction program focused on rehabilitation.

senses.definition: An amount or quantity of something added or subtracted so as to correct.
senses.example: Adding a small correction to the bathroom scale's reading made the weight more accurate.

senses.definition: A decline in a stock market price after a period of rises. Often operationally defined as a market value drop of 10% or more on some specific stock market index.
senses.example: After the tech sell-off, the index posted a correction of more than ten percent in one week.

senses.definition: A station's indication that previous information was incorrect and will continue with correct information from the last correct transmitted.
senses.example: I have four T-80 tanks at grid Three-niner-niner-four-eight-eight, Correction: Grid Three niner-niner-four-eight-five. How copy? Over.

core.definition: The act of fixing or changing something that is wrong, or a change that fixes an error.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on REK. The -tion ending is pronounced 'shun', not 'tee-on'. The first syllable is a weak schwa, so don't say 'cor'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound critical when directed at a person, but is usually positive in technical or editorial use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use correction for fixing a mistake, such as a correction printed in a newspaper or a correction made to a document. In schools and prisons it can also mean discipline or rehabilitation. In everyday speech, fix or mistake is often more natural, and correction sounds formal.

distinctions.note: A correction fixes a specific error; a revision changes or improves a text as a whole, often for a new version.
Correction can mean rehabilitation or discipline meant to improve behavior; punishment focuses on penalty.

examples.everyday: Thanks for the correction, I had the wrong address on the invitation.
examples.professional: Please see the correction in the attached file; the deadline should read March 15, not March 5.
examples.analytical: Augustine treats divine correction as painful but loving, a discipline that aims at the soul's return to God.

nuance.analogy: A correction is like a GPS recalculating your route after you take a wrong turn.
nuance.etymology: From Latin correctio, from corrigere 'to make straight', from com- 'together' and regere 'to guide'.
common_mistakes: Using correction for casual fixes, which sounds stiff; 'fix' or 'mistake' is more natural.
Pronouncing -tion as 'tee-on' instead of 'shun'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the RSV, correction translates several Greek and Hebrew words about discipline and reproof. The Greek epanorthosis appears in Second Timothy 3:16, where Scripture is described as profitable for correction. Hebrews 12:11 uses the Greek paideia, meaning training or discipline, and says that present discipline is painful but yields peaceful fruit. Proverbs 3:11-12 uses the Hebrew musar and tells the reader not to despise the Lord's discipline, since the Lord corrects those he loves.

correction.etymology: From Middle English *correccioun*, *correction*, from Old French *correccion*, from Latin *corrēctiō*.

senses.definition: In cosmetic terms; regarding appearance.

core.definition: In terms of appearance only, not function, structure or health; superficially in looks.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable MET. The first vowel is the American cot vowel, like the a in 'father', not the 'aw' of 'caught'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but 'only cosmetically' can sound dismissive, suggesting the change does not solve the real problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cosmetically in everyday talk about cars, houses, products, repairs and surgery. A phrase like 'cosmetically fine but structurally bad' is common in home inspections and used-car discussions. It usually implies that only the surface has changed.

distinctions.note: Aesthetically concerns beauty and artistic taste; cosmetically concerns surface appearance and changes made to it.
Superficially suggests shallowness or deception; cosmetically is more neutral and literal.

examples.everyday: The used car is cosmetically rough with some dents, but the engine runs perfectly.
examples.professional: The vendor said the update was cosmetically minor, but it actually changed the API contract our partners depend on.
examples.analytical: A policy can be cosmetically reformed while leaving the underlying incentives untouched.

nuance.analogy: Like repainting a rusted car: it looks new until you look underneath.
nuance.etymology: From cosmetic, from Greek kosmetikos, skilled in adorning, from kosmein, to adorn.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable with an aw sound, like 'cawz', instead of the American 'kahz'
Confusing cosmetically with cosmically, which means on a cosmic scale

senses.definition: In a cosmic manner.

core.definition: On a vast, universal scale; in a way that feels enormous, cosmic or fated.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KAHZ, with the American cot vowel. The -ally ending reduces to 'lee' with no separate 'a' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in science, but often hyperbolic or humorous in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cosmically casually for emphasis, as in 'cosmically unfair', and in popular astronomy writing. It sounds dramatic, so use it for big ideas, not small annoyances. In formal or scientific writing, it refers to the scale of the universe.

distinctions.note: Universally means everywhere or for everyone; cosmically suggests vast scale or cosmic significance.
Extremely is a general intensifier; cosmically adds a sense of the enormous or fated.

examples.everyday: Missing the bus by one second felt cosmically unfair, and I told my wife so as I walked home.
examples.professional: The vendor's claim was cosmically overstated; the actual latency difference was milliseconds, not seconds.
examples.analytical: Pascal saw human life as cosmically small, yet he still believed it was infinitely significant to God.

nuance.analogy: Like measuring a single grain of sand against the whole coastline: small on its own, enormous in its place on the scale.
nuance.etymology: From cosmic plus the adverb suffix -ally, from Greek kosmikos, of the world-order.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying kah-ZMIK-lee instead of KAHZ-mih-klee
Using cosmically as a casual synonym for very, which sounds exaggerated in most conversations

senses.definition: In a kitchen, a surface, often built into the wall and above a cabinet, designed to be used for food preparation.
senses.example: She rolled out pizza dough on the kitchen counter while the oven preheated.

senses.definition: In a bathroom, a surface, often built into the wall and above a cabinet, which holds the washbasin.
senses.example: He set his toothbrush on the bathroom counter next to the sink.

senses.definition: One who counts.
senses.example: He's only 16 months, but is already a good counter – he can count to 100.

senses.definition: A reckoner; someone who collects data by counting; an enumerator.
senses.example: The census counter knocked on every door in the neighborhood to tally residents.

senses.definition: An object (now especially a small disc) used in counting or keeping count, or as a marker in games, etc.
senses.example: He rolled a six on the dice, so moved his counter forward six spaces.

senses.definition: A telltale; a contrivance attached to an engine, printing press, or other machine, for the purpose of counting the revolutions or the pulsations.
senses.example: The mechanic checked the engine's revolution counter to see how many times the crankshaft had turned.

senses.definition: A variable, memory location, etc. whose contents are incremented to keep a count.
senses.example: The loop uses a counter variable that increments by one after each pass through the array.

senses.definition: A hit counter.
senses.example: Our blog's hit counter jumped to ten thousand after the article was shared online.

senses.definition: A table or board on which money is counted and over which business is transacted.
senses.example: He put his money on the counter, and the shopkeeper put it in the till.

senses.definition: A shop tabletop on which goods are examined, weighed or measured.
senses.example: The jeweler placed the ring on the glass counter under a bright lamp for inspection.

senses.definition: Any stone lying closer to the center than any of the opponent's stones.
senses.example: In the final end, Marta's stone sat as the counter closest to the button.

senses.definition: A class of word used along with numbers to count objects and events, typically mass nouns. Although rare and optional in English (e.g. "20 head of cattle"), they are numerous and required in Chinese, Japanese, and Korean.
senses.example: In Japanese, you must add a counter after numbers when counting flat objects like sheets of paper.

senses.definition: Something opposite or contrary to something else.
senses.example: Her quiet patience was the perfect counter to his constant impatience at meetings.

senses.definition: A proactive defensive hold or move in reaction to a hold or move by one's opponent.
senses.example: Always know a counter to any hold you try against your opponent.

senses.definition: The piece of a shoe or a boot around the heel of the foot (above the heel of the shoe/boot).
senses.example: The boot's counter had cracked, so the heel slid around inside her shoe.

senses.definition: The breast of a horse; that part of a horse between the shoulders and under the neck.
senses.example: The vet pressed gently on the horse's counter, feeling for tenderness before fitting the new saddle.

senses.definition: The enclosed or partly closed negative space of a glyph.
senses.example: Tiny fonts can fill the counter of a lowercase e with ink and blur it.

senses.definition: Counterattack.
senses.example: The defenders launched a counter just before halftime and nearly scored.

senses.definition: The overhanging stern of a vessel above the waterline, below and somewhat forward of the stern proper.
senses.example: The yacht's counter overhangs the water behind the transom, catching light on its polished wood.

senses.definition: (historical) The prison attached to a city court; a compter.
senses.example: Debtors in eighteenth-century London were often locked in the Counter until family paid.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: Contrary, in opposition; in an opposite direction.
In the wrong way; contrary to the right course.
senses.example: a hound that runs counter

senses.definition: To contradict, oppose.
To return a blow while receiving one, as in boxing.
To take action in response to; to respond.
Contrary or opposing.
senses.example: His carrying a knife was counter to my plan.

core.definition: A long flat surface in a kitchen, restaurant or store where food is prepared, served, ordered or paid for.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The t between vowels is often a flap, so it sounds like 'KOWN-der', and the final er is a weak American r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word for a physical surface or service area.
nuance.usage_note: In American restaurants, the counter often means the service area where you order, as in 'Order at the counter and we'll bring it to your table.' At home, the counter is the kitchen countertop. Americans also say checkout counter in stores. Sitting at a counter is a casual dining option, while a bar usually serves alcohol.

distinctions.note: Countertop is the surface itself in a home kitchen; counter can also mean the service point in a restaurant or store.
A bar usually serves drinks and has stools facing the bartender, while a counter often serves food or coffee.
A cabinet stores items below or above the counter; the counter is the working surface you prepare food on.

examples.everyday: Just leave the mail on the kitchen counter, and I'll sort it later.
examples.professional: Our store manager asked us to restock the returns counter before the weekend rush.
examples.analytical: The counter in a fast-food line is designed as a transaction point, which shapes how customers queue, decide and pay.

nuance.analogy: A counter is like a stage between the kitchen and the customer, where the work is shown and exchanged.
nuance.etymology: From Old French conteor, a table for counting money, from Latin computare, 'to count'.
common_mistakes: Saying counter for a bar stool; a counter is the surface or service area, not the seating at a bar.
Pronouncing it with a long o sound or 'count-er' as two strong syllables.

counter.etymology: Middle English *countour*, from Old French *conteor* (French *comptoir*), from Medieval Latin *computātōrium*, from Latin *computō*, equivalent to *count* + *er*.

conversation.text: Order at the counter, and they'll bring the food to your table.
We sat at the counter and watched the cooks make our pancakes.
Just leave the groceries on the counter, and I'll put them away.

senses.definition: A conditional statement in which the conditional clause is false.
senses.example: A counterfactual like 'If I had studied harder, I would have passed' is false.

senses.definition: A claim, hypothesis, or other belief that is contrary to the facts.
senses.example: Historians dismiss his claim that the war was won by a single battle as a counterfactual.

senses.definition: A hypothetical state of the world, used to assess the impact of an action.
senses.example: Our economists built a counterfactual in which the tariff never passed, to measure its effect on jobs.

senses.definition: Contrary to known or agreed facts; untrue.
senses.example: Her counterfactual claims about the election were simply untrue, and the records prove it.

senses.definition: Of or in comparison to a hypothetical state of the world.
senses.example: The counterfactual model estimated how wages would have changed without the minimum wage increase.

core.definition: Describing a situation or statement that is contrary to what actually happened, used to explore what would have occurred otherwise.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on FAK, the third syllable. The 'tu' in 'factual' is pronounced like 'choo', and the ending is reduced to 'uhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and analytical. It is a precise term in research and does not carry an emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in philosophy, economics, statistics, data science, and policy analysis, especially when talking about 'what if' scenarios. In everyday speech, people more often say 'hypothetical' or 'what if'. Counterfactual is common in academic writing and in technical talks about causal inference.

distinctions.note: Hypothetical means imagined or supposed in general, while counterfactual specifically refers to something contrary to known facts.
Speculative describes guesses about the future or unknown matters, while counterfactual deals with alternate pasts or states of the world.
Fictional means made up for stories, while counterfactual is used as a reasoning tool in analysis.

examples.everyday: Do you ever wonder what your life would be like if you had moved to another city, that counterfactual kind of thinking?
examples.professional: The model compares actual sales with the counterfactual sales we would have seen without the new ad campaign.
examples.analytical: Causal claims in history depend on counterfactual reasoning, since we must imagine how events would have unfolded without a key decision.

nuance.analogy: Like a parallel timeline in a video game where you ask what would have happened if you had chosen the other door.
nuance.etymology: From counter- (contrary) plus factual, from Latin factum (something done).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'coun-ter-FAC-chuh-ul' with the wrong vowel; the first vowel is a diphthong 'ow'.
Using it to mean 'false' in general; it means contrary to known facts in a hypothetical way.

senses.definition: Highly sought-after.
senses.example: The corner office was the most coveted spot on the entire fourth floor.

core.definition: Strongly desired by many people, often because it seems valuable, rare, or prestigious.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KUV. The ending -ed is pronounced as a separate short syllable 'id' because it follows the t sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it suggests that others want something, often with a hint of envy or competition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coveted in both casual and professional speech, especially for jobs, prizes, seats, and status symbols. It implies that many others want the same thing. A natural phrase is a highly coveted spot or one of the most coveted positions.

distinctions.note: Desired is the general, neutral word for wanting something, while coveted stresses strong envy or competition for it.
Prized emphasizes the high value someone places on something, while coveted emphasizes that others also want it.
Envied describes the feeling of others toward a person or possession, while coveted describes the object of desire.

examples.everyday: That corner table at the diner is the most coveted seat in town.
examples.professional: The data science role is highly coveted, so the hiring panel reviewed over two hundred applications.
examples.analytical: Scholars have long regarded a coveted prize such as tenure as a signal of institutional status rather than of merit alone.

nuance.analogy: A coveted item is like the last slice of pizza at a party: everyone is eyeing it at once.
nuance.etymology: Past participle adjective from covet, from Old French coveitier (to desire eagerly), from Latin cupere (to desire).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as two syllables (KUVD) instead of three (KUV-ih-tid).
Confusing coveted with covert or covenant in spelling and speech.
Using coveted for everyday things that are not especially in demand.

senses.definition: Initialism of charge, parity, time-reversal (in the phrase CPT symmetry).
Abbreviation of carpet. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: Our flooring quote lists CPT for the bedrooms and tile for the bathroom.

senses.definition: Initialism of Colored People's Time.
Initialism of cost per thousand.
senses.example: The ad agency reported that our campaign's CPT dropped to under four dollars this quarter.

senses.definition: Initialism of Carriage Paid To.
senses.example: Shipping terms on the invoice read CPT Chicago, so the seller covers freight.

core.definition: Initialism for charge, parity and time reversal: a physics symmetry saying the laws of physics stay unchanged when all three are reversed together.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters one by one: 'see', 'pee', 'tee'. The primary stress falls on the last letter, 'TEE', and each letter keeps its full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term in physics.
nuance.usage_note: In American physics, CPT symmetry is a technical term used in research and graduate courses. In shipping, 'CPT' is the abbreviation for 'Carriage Paid To', a trade term on invoices meaning the seller pays freight to a named destination. 'Colored People's Time' is an old, racist joke suggesting Black people are habitually late; avoid it entirely. 'CPT' is not an abbreviation for 'carpet' in standard American English, so do not use it that way.

distinctions.note: CP violation is the breaking of charge-parity symmetry, observed in particle decays; CPT symmetry is believed to hold exactly, with time reversal included.
Carriage Paid To is a shipping term about who pays freight, and it has nothing to do with physics.

examples.everyday: My physics friend keeps talking about CPT symmetry, and I just nod along.
examples.professional: Our physics collaborator says the detector results would be meaningless if CPT symmetry were violated.
examples.analytical: Any Lorentz-invariant quantum field theory with a local Hamiltonian must respect CPT symmetry, which makes any observed violation so significant.

nuance.analogy: CPT symmetry is like a movie that looks the same when you play it in reverse, swap the characters and flip the mirror image.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of 'charge', 'parity' and 'time'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'see-pee-tay' with the stress on the first letter; the stress is on the last letter.
Using 'CPT' for 'carpet', which is not a standard American abbreviation.

senses.definition: Excessive emphasis on the importance of educational, academic, legal, or regulatory qualifications.
senses.example: Her firm's credentialism meant that talented people without degrees never got interviews.

core.definition: Excessive reliance on degrees, certificates and other formal qualifications when judging whether someone is able to do a job.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DEN, and the -tial syllable reduces to shuh. Many learners say cre-DEN-shee-al-ism; the American form is shorter and ends in a weak schwa-l.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Speakers use it to criticize hiring or promotion rules that demand degrees even when they are not needed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use credentialism in debates about hiring, licensing and education, especially when a degree is required for a job that does not need one. It sounds critical, so use it when you want to point out a problem, not to describe a normal requirement. In a meeting you might say 'We're being credentialist about this role' to argue for hiring on skills.

distinctions.note: Credentialing is the neutral process of verifying qualifications; credentialism is the excessive emphasis on them.
A meritocracy rewards demonstrated ability; credentialism can be a barrier to merit when it demands formal credentials that are not needed.

examples.everyday: My brother can fix any engine, but he got turned down for the job because he doesn't have a certificate, which is pure credentialism.
examples.professional: Our job postings should not require a four-year degree unless the work truly needs one, or we risk credentialism that limits our candidate pool.
examples.analytical: Credentialism mistakes a proxy for competence, treating the signal of a diploma as if it were the capacity it was meant to certify.

nuance.analogy: Credentialism is like judging a chef only by the name of the culinary school on their résumé, never by tasting the food.
nuance.etymology: From credential, from medieval Latin credentialis 'giving confidence', from Latin credere 'to believe', plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: the stress is on DEN, not on the last syllable.
Using credentialism to mean any credential; it refers to the excessive emphasis on credentials.

senses.definition: A crack or fissure in a glacier or snowfield; a chasm.
A breach in a canal or river bank.
senses.example: After the spring storms, the river broke through a weak spot and formed a crevasse near the farm.

senses.definition: Any cleft or fissure.
A discontinuity or “gap” between the accounted variables and an observed outcome.
senses.example: The model's residuals revealed a crevasse between predicted churn rates and what customers actually did.

senses.definition: To form crevasses.
senses.example: Years of drought caused the dry clay to crevasse into deep cracks across the valley floor.

senses.definition: To fissure with crevasses.
senses.example: Meltwater and heavy traffic gradually crevassed the glacier's surface, making the trail dangerous for hikers.

core.definition: A deep, narrow crack or fissure in a glacier or snowfield, often hidden under snow and dangerous to climbers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VASS. The final -sse is pronounced like the vowel in mass, not like ass with a long a, and the first syllable is a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or cautionary, because it refers to a hazard in mountaineering and polar travel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use crevasse mainly in mountaineering, polar exploration and glaciology. Hikers and climbers talk about hidden crevasses on glaciers. In general speech a crack or deep crack is more common for ordinary breaks in ground or ice.

distinctions.note: A crevice is a small, narrow opening in rock or a wall, while a crevasse is a much larger, deep fissure in ice.
A chasm is a very deep gap, often in rock, while a crevasse specifically refers to a crack in ice or snow.

examples.everyday: The guide told us to stay on the marked trail because there were hidden crevasses everywhere.
examples.professional: The survey team flagged a new crevasse near base camp, so we need to reroute the supply line.
examples.analytical: Crevasses form where tensile stress in flowing ice exceeds the strength of the ice.

nuance.analogy: Like a crack in a frozen pond, but deep enough to swallow a climber.
nuance.etymology: From French crevasse, a crack, from crevasser, to crack.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as KREV-ass or kruh-VAH-zuh
Confusing crevasse with crevice when describing rock formations

senses.definition: The state or condition of being crimson in color.

core.definition: The quality or state of being crimson, a deep, rich red color with a slight blue tint.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, KRIMZ-, and the middle syllable is a reduced uh. Do not give the -son- part a full vowel as in 'son'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to vivid. It evokes intense color, blood, passion, or danger, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'crimsonness' in conversation. They say 'the crimson color' or simply 'bright red.' The word appears mainly in literary description, poetry, and art criticism.

distinctions.note: Scarlet is an orange-red, while crimson is deeper and has a bluish tint.
Red is the everyday color word, while crimsonness is a rare literary noun for the quality of crimson.

examples.professional: The paint sample's crimsonness was too intense for the nursery, so the designer suggested a softer shade.
examples.analytical: The poem's repeated crimsonness links violence and desire, so the color carries both danger and longing.

nuance.analogy: Like the richest red wine in a glass, crimsonness is red deepened into a darker, more intense hue.
nuance.etymology: From crimson, from Medieval Latin cremesinus, ultimately from Arabic and Persian words for a red dye, plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using 'crimsonness' in casual talk; 'bright red' or 'the crimson color' is more natural.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'son' rather than a reduced uh.

senses.definition: A scheduler or timer that automatically starts a job, program, task.
senses.example: I set a cron job to back up the database every night at midnight.

core.definition: A scheduler on Unix-like systems that automatically runs commands or scripts at set times or intervals.

pronunciation.tip: Say it as one syllable, KRAHN, rhyming with 'con' or 'Don'. Americans use the cot vowel here, not the 'aw' of 'caught'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a neutral technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers say 'cron' for the Unix job scheduler and call the schedule itself a 'cron job' or 'cron expression'. In meetings, people might say 'the nightly cron' or 'put it on cron'. Outside tech, the word means nothing, so explain it if needed.

distinctions.note: Scheduler is a general term for any system that runs tasks at set times; cron is one specific Unix scheduler.
A systemd timer is a newer alternative on Linux; cron is the older, long-standing standard.

examples.everyday: My laptop backs up the photos every night because of a cron job I set up years ago.
examples.professional: The data pipeline runs as a cron job at 2 a.m., so check the logs if the report is missing.
examples.analytical: A cron job is a stateless scheduler: it fires at a time, not in response to the state of the system.

nuance.analogy: Cron is like an alarm clock for a computer: it wakes up a program at the same time every day.
nuance.etymology: Short for 'chronos', Greek for 'time', via the Unix scheduler named cron.
common_mistakes: Saying 'crone' for 'cron', which means an old woman.
Pronouncing it with the 'aw' vowel as 'KRAWN'.

senses.definition: A bird, usually black, of the genus Corvus, having a strong conical beak, with projecting bristles; it has a harsh, croaking call.
senses.example: A lone crow sat on the fence post, cawing at the tractor as it rolled past the barn.

senses.definition: Any of various dark-colored nymphalid butterflies of the genus Euploea.
senses.example: Collectors prize the crow butterflies of Southeast Asia for their deep, glossy wings.

senses.definition: A bar of iron with a beak, crook or claw; a bar of iron used as a lever; a crowbar.
senses.example: He pried the rotted boards loose with a crow and a claw hammer.

senses.definition: A gangplank (corvus) used by the Ancient Roman navy to board enemy ships.
senses.example: Roman sailors lowered the crow onto the enemy deck, locking the ships together for boarding.

senses.definition: The mesentery of an animal.
senses.example: The butcher explained that the crow is the thin membrane that holds the intestines in place.

senses.definition: An ill-tempered and obstinate woman, or one who otherwise has features resembling the bird; a harpy.
senses.example: Don't mind her, she's an old crow, but she knows every rule in this building.

senses.definition: A black person.
The cry or call of a rooster or a cockerel, especially as heard at sunrise.
senses.example: At dawn, the rooster's crow woke the whole farm before the sun cleared the hills.

senses.definition: The emblem of an eagle, a sign of military rank.
senses.example: The colonel's shoulder bore the silver crow, marking him as a full colonel.

senses.definition: (rare) Someone who keeps watch while their associates commit a crime; a lookout.
senses.example: While his partner cracked the safe, Danny stood outside as the crow, watching for police cars.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: To use a crowbar, wedge, or other implement to attempt to open a surface by leveraging force on the opposite end of the tool to pry off the connection between the two surfaces.
senses.example: If you wanna get inside, you're gonna have to crow open that door.

senses.definition: To make the shrill sound characteristic of a rooster; to make a sound in this manner, either in gaiety, joy, pleasure, or defiance.
senses.example: The rooster crowed at sunrise, and the farmer grumbled that the bird never let him sleep.

senses.definition: To shout in exultation or defiance; to brag.
senses.example: He’s been crowing all day about winning the game of cards.

senses.definition: To test the reed of a double reed instrument by placing the reed alone in the mouth and blowing it.
senses.example: Before the lesson, she crowed the reed alone, checking whether it sounded stable and responsive.

senses.definition: (uncommon) Dark black, the color of a crow; crow-black.
senses.example: Her hair was crow black, glossy and so dark it seemed to swallow the lamplight.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: A large black bird with a harsh, cawing call, often seen in fields and parks.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long 'oh' vowel: KROH. Make the r clear at the start, and do not add a vowel between the k and the r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in ordinary talk. The bird can be seen as an omen or a pest, depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly use crow for the bird in everyday talk about nature, farms, and birdwatching. The verb crow is used for a rooster's call, and in informal speech for bragging or gloating, as in 'Don't crow about it.' Crow is not the word for a pigeon or a raven, though the raven is a related large black bird.

distinctions.note: A raven is a larger bird with a deeper, croaking call and a heavier bill, while a crow is smaller and more common in towns and fields.
A crowbar is the metal lever tool, while crow in the old sense of a tool is a rare, technical term for a bar with a beak or claw.

examples.everyday: A flock of crows keeps landing in our backyard oak every morning.
examples.professional: The farm report mentioned crows eating newly planted seed, so we should set up netting.
examples.analytical: In many cultures the crow symbolizes ill omen, though some traditions treat it as a clever trickster.

nuance.analogy: A crow is like a black paper cutout on the sky, easy to spot and loud in its call.
nuance.etymology: From Old English crawe, of Germanic origin, imitating the bird's call.
common_mistakes: Confusing crow with raven, since both are large black birds.
Using crow as a verb for any bird sound, when it is mainly a rooster's call or informal bragging.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, the Hebrew word orev and the Greek word korax refer to ravens, and the RSV generally translates them as raven rather than crow. Scripture does mention God's care for birds, where the Greek korakas, for ravens, appears. Luke 12:24 says God feeds the ravens, which the RSV renders as ravens, and Genesis 8:7 describes Noah sending out a raven from the ark. Matthew 26:34 uses the image of a cock crowing, which is a rooster's call rather than a crow.

crow.etymology: From Middle English *crowe*, from Old English *crāwe*, from **krāā*, from Proto-Germanic **krēǭ*, from **krēaną* (“to crow”).

senses.definition: A regular polyhedron having six identical square faces.
senses.example: When the math teacher is teaching the class about cubes, he asks them to imagine a cardboard box whose width, length, and height are all the same.

senses.definition: Any object more or less in the form of a cube.
senses.example: A: One cube or two? B: Oh, no sugar for me, thanks.

senses.definition: The third power of a number, value, term or expression.
senses.example: The cube of 2 is 8.

senses.definition: A data structure consisting of a three-dimensional array; a data cube.
senses.example: The analyst queried the sales data cube to compare revenue across regions and years.

senses.definition: A Rubik's cube style puzzle, not necessarily in the shape of a cube.
senses.example: He spent the flight twisting a cube puzzle, trying to match all the colors on each face.

senses.definition: Clipping of cubic inch(es).
