(Can we verify this sense?) To castrate; to geld; to emasculate.
(historical) A mass of matted hair worn down over the eyes, formerly common in Ireland.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Speaking smoothly and easily but without sincerity, careful thought, or real knowledge.

pronunciation.tip: One short vowel, like the 'i' in 'big'. End with a clear 'b' sound, and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes someone for having an easy answer to a hard question.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glib to describe a person, a remark, or an explanation that sounds slick but lacks depth. Saying 'That's a glib answer' is a polite but firm criticism. It is not normally used for someone who speaks well and knows the subject.

distinctions.note: Fluent is positive and describes smooth speech in a language or topic. Glib is critical and suggests the smoothness hides a lack of thought.
Superficial describes a lack of depth in a topic or person. Glib focuses on how the talk sounds, especially its easy confidence.

examples.everyday: Don't give me that glib excuse. Just tell me what really happened.
examples.professional: The vendor gave a glib answer about data security, so I want written details before we sign anything.
examples.analytical: A glib account of moral complexity can make the hardest questions seem easy, which is exactly why it is dangerous.

nuance.analogy: Like a salesman whose smile promises more than the product can deliver.
nuance.etymology: Probably from Middle English glibbe, meaning smooth or slippery, of Low German or Dutch origin.
common_mistakes: Using glib as a compliment for clever speech. It is usually a criticism.
Confusing glib with quick or clever. Glib implies speed without substance.

glib.etymology: A shortening of either obsolete or its source, *glibberig* (“slippery”) / Dutch *glibberig* (“slippery”).

senses.definition: A figure carved in relief or incised, especially representing a sound, word, or idea.
Any of various figures used in Mayan writing.
senses.example: The archaeologist deciphered the glyph carved on the temple stela.

senses.definition: Any non-verbal symbol that imparts information.
senses.example: The app uses a small glyph to show when a message has been read.

senses.definition: A visual representation of a letter, character, or symbol, in a specific font and style.
senses.example: The grid column header displays a sort glyph indicating an ascending or descending ordering.

senses.definition: A vertical groove.
senses.example: Each column has twenty-four glyphs cut into its shaft.

senses.definition: A land snail of the genus Glyphyalinia.
senses.example: The field team found a glyph snail hiding under wet leaves in the forest.

senses.definition: Any of various black-and-white noctuid moths with figural-like wing patterns, such as those in Protodeltote, Deltote, and Maliattha.
senses.example: The collector pinned a glyph moth beside the other noctuids in the drawer.

core.definition: A carved or drawn symbol that represents a sound, word, or idea, as in ancient writing such as Mayan or Egyptian.

pronunciation.tip: The g is hard, as in 'go', and the vowel is short, like 'lip'. The ph is pronounced f, and there is no extra vowel between g and l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a descriptive term for symbols and is used without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glyph mostly in archaeology, linguistics, and typography, where it refers to a single carved or drawn sign. In everyday talk people say symbol or character. In computing, a glyph is the visual shape of a character in a font, so you might hear 'the glyph for the letter a'.

distinctions.note: A symbol is any sign that stands for something, while a glyph specifically means a carved or drawn sign, often in writing.
A hieroglyph is a specific kind of glyph in Egyptian writing; glyph is the broader term.
A character is a unit of a writing system, while a glyph is the physical shape used to write that character.

examples.everyday: The old map had little animal glyphs in the corners that I couldn't read.
examples.professional: Our OCR model keeps misreading the stylized glyphs in the scanned manuscripts.
examples.analytical: Mayan glyphs combine sound and meaning, so they cannot be read simply as pictures.

nuance.analogy: A glyph is like a road sign: its shape carries a message even without any spoken words.
nuance.etymology: From French glyphe, from Greek glyphē, 'carving', from glyphein, 'to carve'.
common_mistakes: Confusing glyph with hieroglyph; hieroglyph is a specific kind of Egyptian glyph.
Pronouncing the ph as p, as in 'glip'; it is an f sound.

senses.definition: To grind (one's teeth) in pain or in anger.
senses.example: gnashing your teeth

senses.definition: To grind between the teeth.
senses.example: to gnash the air in fury

senses.definition: To clash together violently.
senses.example: Stress made him gnash his teeth through the night, so his dentist fitted a guard.

senses.definition: A sudden snapping of the teeth.
senses.example: The dog gave a sudden gnash of its jaws, and the mail carrier stepped back.

core.definition: To grind or clench the teeth together, especially in anger, pain or distress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the single syllable. The g is silent, so start directly with the n sound, and keep the vowel short like in cash.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting intense suffering, rage or despair.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this in the Bible, in literature or in phrases like 'gnash your teeth'. In everyday speech they would say 'grind your teeth' or 'clench your jaw'. The phrase is dramatic, so it works best in serious or stylized writing.

distinctions.note: Grind is everyday and can describe teeth during sleep, while gnash suggests a violent, emotional clenching.
Clench means to tighten the jaw or fist, whereas gnash specifically involves grinding teeth in pain or anger.

examples.everyday: I was so frustrated in traffic that I could only gnash my teeth and wait.
examples.professional: Stakeholders were gnashing their teeth over the delayed release, so we should send a clear update.
examples.analytical: The text uses gnash to render raw grief, making the body speak where words fail.

nuance.analogy: Like two millstones grinding against each other with nothing to crush, producing sound and friction.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English gnasshen, probably of imitative origin.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the initial g, as in G-NASH.
Confusing it with gnaw, which means biting persistently.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Gospels the Greek word brygmos (grinding, gnashing of teeth) describes the suffering of those cast into outer darkness, as in Matthew 8:12 and Matthew 13:42. The Hebrew charaq appears in Psalm 35:16, where enemies gnash their teeth at the psalmist, and in Psalm 112:10, where the wicked gnash their teeth and melt away.

gnash.etymology: From Middle English *gnasten*. the word is probably either Germanic or ultimately.

senses.definition: Having the characteristics of a god.
Characteristic of a god.
senses.example: Her godlike composure during the crisis impressed everyone in the emergency room.

core.definition: Having qualities that are like those of a god, such as being extremely powerful, skilled, or impressive.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GOD. The final syllable -like rhymes with 'bike', and the 'd' before l is light, so say GAHD-lyke, not GOD-lik.

nuance.connotation: Positive or admiring when praising skill, power, or beauty; negative when describing arrogance or claims to superiority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use godlike to praise extraordinary ability, often in sports, music or technology, with a bit of exaggeration. It is a strong compliment, so use it sparingly. In religious contexts, speakers say divine or godly instead to avoid suggesting that a human is literally a god.

distinctions.note: Godly describes a person who is pious or devoted to God; godlike describes qualities like a god's power, not religious devotion.
Divine can mean excellent in casual speech, but it is more formal and more religious; godlike is more hyperbolic and secular.

examples.everyday: My buddy fixes cars with godlike skill; he can hear what's wrong just by listening to the engine.
examples.professional: The new model's godlike accuracy on the benchmark looks too good to be true, so we should check for data leakage before we celebrate.
examples.analytical: Hegel's Absolute is often described in godlike terms, though he resisted identifying it with a personal deity of the Christian kind.

nuance.analogy: Godlike is like calling a chef's cooking 'heavenly': the word lifts the praise above ordinary human skill.
nuance.etymology: From god plus -like, meaning 'resembling'.
common_mistakes: Using godlike to describe religious piety; for that, say godly.
Stressing the final syllable, as in 'god-LIKE'; the stress is on GOD.

senses.definition: A period of time in the distant past when things were better or fondly remembered.
senses.example: In the good old days we could go to the gasworks and buy coke.

core.definition: A period in the past, often idealized, when life seemed better, simpler or happier than it is now.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DAYS, with old getting a lighter secondary stress. The l in old is clearly pronounced, and the final s in days is a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Nostalgic and usually warm, though it can be used ironically to complain about the present.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say back in the good old days when talking about childhood, earlier jobs or past technology, often with a fond or joking tone. It is usually plural and fixed; say the good old days, not the good old day. A natural reply is 'Yeah, those were the days,' or 'I miss those days too.'

distinctions.note: Nostalgia is a feeling of longing for the past; good old days names a specific idealized period.
Heyday refers to the peak of a person's or thing's success, not an idealized past in general.
Back in the day is more casual American slang and can refer to any past period, including recent ones.

collocations: back in the good old days
talk about the good old days
those were the good old days

examples.everyday: Back in the good old days, we just called each other on the landline and didn't have to text.
examples.professional: We used to ship releases quarterly in the good old days, but now we deploy several times a day.
examples.analytical: Appeals to the good old days often idealize a past whose hardships have been forgotten.

nuance.analogy: The good old days are like an old photograph: the colors look warmer than the original moment felt.
common_mistakes: Using the singular good old day, which is not the fixed American form.
Using good old days for a literal past period without any fond or joking feeling.

core.definition: A title for Jesus, who cares for his people as a shepherd cares for sheep and who gives his life for them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SHEP, and the second syllable is a weak, r-colored 'erd', so say 'SHEP-erd' with two syllables. Do not add an extra vowel between 'p' and 'r'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it expresses warm comfort, protection and devoted care.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this title in churches, hymns, Bible studies and Christian art. In secular speech it is rarely used except as a reference to the Bible. Good Shepherd Sunday is the fourth Sunday of Easter in many churches, when this passage from John 10 is read.

distinctions.note: John 10 contrasts the good shepherd, who protects the sheep, with the hired hand, who runs away when danger comes.

collocations: lay down his life as the Good Shepherd

examples.everyday: Our pastor's sermon on John 10 really stuck with me, the idea of Jesus as the Good Shepherd.
examples.professional: In my teaching series, I contrast the hired hand with Christ, the Good Shepherd, in John 10.
examples.analytical: The Johannine good shepherd discourse presents Jesus's self-giving death as the defining mark of divine care.

nuance.analogy: Like a parent who stays up all night with a sick child, the Good Shepherd keeps watch over his flock.
nuance.etymology: Drawn from John 10:11, where Jesus calls himself the good shepherd; Greek kalos means good, beautiful or noble.
common_mistakes: Using lowercase 'good shepherd' when referring to Jesus in a religious context, where capitals are expected.
Pronouncing 'Shepherd' with a long e, as in 'SHEEP-herd'.
nuance.biblical_note: Jesus calls himself the good shepherd in John 10:11-14, the Greek is poimēn kalos (ποιμὴν καλός). Key passages: John 10:11, where he says the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep; John 10:12-13, where the hired hand flees from the wolf because the sheep are not his own; and Psalm 23:1, where the Lord is the shepherd who cares for his people.

senses.definition: A soldier in a small independent group, fighting against the government or regular forces by surprise raids.
senses.example: The right-wing paramilitary's offensive against the Marxist guerrillas failed because they did not know the terrain well enough.

senses.definition: A marketer who uses guerrilla marketing techniques.
senses.example: The agency hired a guerrilla to plaster the subway with stickers for the shoe brand.

senses.definition: A maker of guerrilla television.
senses.example: The documentary was made by a guerrilla who filmed in the streets without permits.

senses.definition: (rare) A non-official war carried out by small independent groups; a guerrilla war.
senses.example: The guerrilla dragged on for a decade in the hills after the treaty collapsed.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Relating to, using, or typical of guerrilla warfare, or its principles of small independent or non-official perpetrators.
senses.example: Our startup ran a guerrilla campaign with flash mobs and chalk drawings downtown.

senses.definition: Relating to, using, or typical of guerrilla marketing.
senses.example: Our startup ran a guerrilla campaign with flash mobs and chalk drawings downtown.

senses.definition: Using unconventional, non-traditional, non-mainstream and often subversive practices to achieve something.
senses.example: guerrilla marketing

core.definition: A member of a small, independent armed group that fights a larger army or government using surprise raids and ambushes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the middle syllable, RIL, and the first and last syllables are weak schwas. Do not say 'gorilla' with an 'or' sound at the start, and do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Often negative or politically charged in war reporting, but neutral or even positive in phrases like guerrilla marketing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use guerrilla most often for irregular fighters in war, especially in news about insurgents. In business and culture, guerrilla marketing and guerrilla gardening mean low-budget, unconventional efforts. Be careful using it for people in a conflict, since it can sound politically loaded; insurgent or rebel are common alternatives.

distinctions.note: Rebel is a broad term for anyone opposing authority, while guerrilla specifically means small irregular fighters using hit-and-run tactics.
Insurgent is a formal political term for someone rising against a government, while guerrilla describes the group or the fighting style.
Terrorist usually means attacks aimed at civilians to create fear, while guerrilla refers to tactics against military forces, though these labels are often contested.

examples.everyday: We pulled off a guerrilla photo shoot in the park with no permit and no big crew.
examples.professional: Our guerrilla marketing campaign got more attention than the paid ads, and it cost almost nothing.
examples.analytical: Guerrilla warfare depends on mobility, local support, and asymmetry, which is why conventional armies often struggle to win.

nuance.analogy: Like a fast, scrappy pickup team that beats a bigger league side with speed and surprise, a guerrilla force wins through agility rather than size.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish guerrilla, meaning little war, from guerra (war).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable or saying GAIR-uh instead of guh-RIL-uh.
Using guerrilla as a general word for any unusual idea without the military or marketing sense.

guerrilla.etymology: Spanish *guerrilla*, diminutive of *guerra* (“war”), coined during the Peninsular War.

senses.definition: Initialism of graphical user interface.

core.definition: Graphical user interface: the system of windows, icons, menus and buttons used to operate a computer or app on screen.

pronunciation.tip: Most Americans in tech say it as one word, 'gooey', rhyming with the adjective. Some say the letters G-U-I, but the spelled-out form is less common in everyday speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it carries no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In software and IT conversation, Americans use 'GUI' in both speech and writing, as in 'the new GUI' or 'a GUI-based tool.' Saying 'gooey' is normal among developers, while spelling out the letters can sound slightly more precise in a formal presentation. Either pronunciation is understood, so match the people around you.

distinctions.note: UI means user interface in general, including voice, text or hardware controls; GUI refers specifically to graphical screens.
A GUI uses windows and icons, while a CLI (command-line interface) uses typed text commands.
A web app is software delivered through a browser, which may or may not have a GUI; GUI describes the visual design layer.

examples.everyday: The new app has a clean GUI, so my dad can finally use it without calling me.
examples.professional: Please review the GUI mockups before Thursday's sprint planning meeting so we can lock the layout.
examples.analytical: The shift from command lines to the GUI changed who could operate computers, turning technical skill into visual navigation.

nuance.analogy: A GUI is like a car dashboard: you press buttons and turn dials instead of wiring the engine yourself.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of graphical user interface.
common_mistakes: Using 'GUI' for any user interface, including voice or text-based ones.
Saying the letters in a team that always says 'gooey', or the reverse, which can sound unfamiliar to colleagues.

senses.definition: The act of tasting.
The ability to taste flavors; the sense of taste.

core.definition: The sense of taste, or the process by which the tongue and mouth detect flavors; a technical word for tasting.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -TAY-, and the ending is the unstressed -shun. Don't stress the first syllable as in 'GUS-ta-tion,' and don't pronounce the middle vowel as a long 'ay' in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a clinical or scientific word with no emotional coloring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use gustation in conversation. In everyday speech they say taste or sense of taste. You will meet it in medicine, neuroscience, food science and sensory analysis, for example 'impaired gustation after chemotherapy.' If you use it at a dinner table it will sound overly technical.

distinctions.note: Taste is the everyday word for both the sense and the flavor of a food. Gustation names the sense itself in a technical or formal context.
Palate can mean the roof of the mouth or a person's ability to appreciate flavor, as in 'a refined palate.' Gustation refers only to the sensory process.

examples.everyday: Since I had the flu, my gustation has been off, so everything tastes flat.
examples.professional: Our sensory panel measured gustation thresholds for bitterness across the three formulations before we chose one.
examples.analytical: Aristotle classed taste with touch, treating gustation as a refined form of tactile contact between the object and the organ.

nuance.analogy: Gustation is the mouth's built-in lab, quietly testing every bite for sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savory.
nuance.etymology: From Latin gustare, 'to taste,' with the suffix -ation.
common_mistakes: Using gustation in everyday conversation, where taste is the natural word.
Confusing the noun gustation with the adjective gustatory, as in 'gustatory nerve' rather than 'gustation nerve'.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to gymnastics.
Of or pertaining to the gymnasia (ancient Greek schools).
senses.example: gymnastic dialogues

core.definition: Relating to gymnastics, or requiring the strength, balance, flexibility, and control that gymnastics demands.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the middle syllable, NAS. The final syllable is short, 'tik', with no long vowel. Keep the 'j' sound at the beginning, as in 'gym'.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gymnastic' with nouns such as 'routine', 'ability', 'moves', or 'skills'. It can be used figuratively for mental or verbal feats, but it sounds slightly literary in that use. Do not use it as a noun; use 'gymnastics' or 'gymnast'.

distinctions.note: 'Gymnastics' is the noun for the sport, while 'gymnastic' is the adjective describing it.
'Acrobatic' refers to flashy, airborne or circus-style movements; 'gymnastic' covers a broader range of controlled exercise moves.

examples.everyday: She has amazing gymnastic moves for someone who started learning at forty.
examples.professional: The gymnastic routine needs better landing sequences before we film it for the promotion.
examples.analytical: The poem's gymnastic syntax forces the reader to rebuild each clause before the meaning settles.

nuance.analogy: A gymnastic movement is like a well-tuned engine: many parts working together with precise control and no wasted motion.
nuance.etymology: From Greek gymnastikos, 'skilled in exercise', from gymnazein, 'to train naked'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I do gymnastic' instead of 'I do gymnastics'.
Stressing the first syllable, which makes the word sound like 'JIM-nas-tik'.

senses.definition: A storm characterized by lots of large hail.

core.definition: A storm in which large pieces of ice, called hail, fall heavily from the sky, often damaging crops, roofs, and cars.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HAYL. Pronounce the r in storm clearly, as American English is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because a hailstorm usually causes damage or disruption. It can be neutral when describing weather in a plain factual way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hailstorm in weather reports, insurance talk, and casual conversation, especially in the Great Plains, Texas, and Colorado, where hail is common. People often say we got hit by a hailstorm or there was a hailstorm last night. The word is more formal than just saying it hailed hard.

distinctions.note: A thunderstorm is any storm with thunder and lightning, while a hailstorm is defined by heavy hail falling, which may or may not include thunder.
A blizzard is a snowstorm with strong winds and low visibility, while a hailstorm involves hail rather than snow.

examples.everyday: We got caught in a hailstorm on the way home, and the car has dents all over the hood now.
examples.professional: The insurance claim covers roof damage from last week's hailstorm, so please send the inspection photos to the adjuster.
examples.analytical: A hailstorm is an extreme weather event whose frequency is hard to attribute to climate trends without long, consistent records.

nuance.analogy: A hailstorm is like a bag of marbles thrown from the sky, with each stone hitting whatever is below.
nuance.etymology: From hail (noun, frozen rain) and storm (noun), from Old English hægel and storm.
common_mistakes: Saying hailstorm for a light sprinkle of ice pellets, when the word implies a heavy, damaging event.
Dropping the r in storm, which is pronounced clearly in American English.

senses.definition: A stickler person who makes extremely, possibly excessively, fine distinctions (who would separate something as fine as a hair into two pieces and distinguish them).
senses.example: My brother is such a hairsplitter that every debate turns into a fight over definitions.

core.definition: A person who makes overly fine or petty distinctions, often arguing about minor points that do not matter.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on HAIR, with a lighter stress on split. The final -er is an unstressed American r-colored vowel, like the ending of 'butter' but with a clear r.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests pedantry and wasted effort, and it is usually used as criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hairsplitter to criticize someone who argues over details that do not matter, often in a meeting or debate. It is informal and can sound rude if said directly to a person. Softer options include let's not split hairs or we're getting into the weeds.

distinctions.note: A nitpicker focuses on small errors to criticize, while a hairsplitter makes subtle distinctions in argument.
A pedant shows off formal knowledge and insists on exact rules, while a hairsplitter argues over fine differences.
A quibbler raises minor objections, while a hairsplitter draws finer and finer logical lines.

examples.everyday: Stop being such a hairsplitter, the restaurant is close enough to the address we gave.
examples.professional: Don't be a hairsplitter about the metric definition, because the dashboard only needs to be accurate enough for the quarterly review.
examples.analytical: A hairsplitter may defend a position by distinguishing meanings few others would notice, which can clarify the argument but also obscure its central claim.

nuance.analogy: Like someone who splits a single hair lengthwise, the hairsplitter divides an issue more finely than anyone needs.
nuance.etymology: From the idiom 'to split hairs', which pictures dividing a single hair into parts.
common_mistakes: Treating hairsplitter as praise for careful thinking, when it usually criticizes excessive fineness.
Stressing both parts equally as hair-SPLIT-er instead of putting the main stress on HAIR.

senses.definition: Consecrated or sanctified; sacred, holy.

core.definition: Regarded as holy or sacred; set apart for worship or respect, often used for places, names, or traditions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The final 'ed' is pronounced as a single 'd' sound, not as a separate syllable, because it follows a vowel sound that is not 't' or 'd'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and reverent. It suggests something deeply respected, often with a sense of tradition or solemnity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hallowed' most often in speeches, eulogies, and writing about a famous place or tradition, such as 'hallowed ground' for a battlefield or cemetery. In casual speech they would say 'sacred' or 'special' instead. It can also be used ironically or humorously in a playful way, but that is uncommon.

distinctions.note: Sacred is the everyday and academic term for religious holiness; hallowed adds a sense of long respect or reverence and is more poetic.
Holy specifically refers to God's nature or to what belongs to God; hallowed describes something made or treated as holy, often by long tradition.

examples.everyday: My uncle calls the old stadium hallowed ground because he saw his first game there as a kid.
examples.professional: The museum director described the restored chapel as hallowed space, and the staff agreed to keep it quiet during tours.
examples.analytical: The phrase hallowed ground in Lincoln's address transforms a battlefield into a site whose sanctity derives from the sacrifice of the dead.

nuance.analogy: Like a family heirloom kept in a special box, something hallowed is treated with reverence because of what it means, not because of its ordinary use.
nuance.etymology: From the past participle of hallow, from Old English hālgian, to make holy.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final 'ed' as a separate syllable ('HAL-oh-ed'); it is one syllable.
Using it for everyday objects, which sounds grandiose or joking.
Confusing it with 'hollowed' (hollowed out), which is spelled and pronounced differently.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses the idea of holiness as being set apart, expressed by the Hebrew qadosh (holy) and the Greek hagios (holy, saint). In Matthew 6:9 of the RSV, the Lord's Prayer begins with the request that God's name be hallowed, which is the sense this adjective carries when describing something treated as holy. The adjective itself is not a Hebrew or Greek word but an English rendering of these ideas.

hallowed.etymology: From Middle English *halwed* (“hallowed, sacred, sanctified”), from Old English *ġehālgod* (“hallowed, sacred, sanctified”), past participle of *hālgian* (“to hallow, make holy”).

core.definition: A major ancient city in northern Syria, on the Orontes River, and a northern landmark of biblical Israel's territory.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, HAY. The final th is voiceless, as in math, not a soft th as in bathe.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a place name used in historical and biblical discussions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet Hamath in Bible study, church history, or ancient geography. It names a city in modern Syria, now usually called Hama. Hama is the modern Arabic-derived name, and the Bible uses Hamath.

distinctions.note: Hama is the modern Syrian city on the same site. Hamath is the biblical and historical name.
Hamon is a different place name, mentioned in Ezekiel. Do not confuse the two.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got curious about the city of Hamath after we read about the northern border of Israel.
examples.professional: In the historical geography section of the lesson, I put Hamath on the map near the Orontes River.
examples.analytical: The northern boundary of Israel, described as reaching to the entrance of Hamath, reflects the ideal extent of the land in the biblical imagination.

nuance.analogy: Think of Hamath as a northern signpost on an old road map, marking where the territory of the kingdom was supposed to end.
nuance.etymology: From a Semitic root, possibly meaning fortress; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like Ham-ath with stress on the second syllable.
Confusing it with the modern city Hama, which is the same site under a different name.
Confusing it with Hamon, another place name in the Bible.
nuance.biblical_note: Hamath is a city in northern Syria on the Orontes River, often mentioned as the northern limit of the land of Israel. Numbers 13:21 describes the spies traveling as far as the entrance of Hamath. 1 Kings 8:65 describes Solomon's assembly stretching from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt. Amos 6:2 uses Hamath as an example of a great city that God will bring judgment upon, showing its prominence to Israel's neighbors.

senses.definition: Having a handicap.
senses.example: handicapped person

senses.definition: Limited by an impediment of some kind.
senses.example: He was handicapped by a bad knee, but he still finished the marathon.

core.definition: Having a physical or mental disability that limits what a person can do. Americans now usually say 'disabled' for people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowels are short and weak, like 'ih', and the word ends with a crisp t sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative or sensitive when describing people. Neutral in set phrases like 'handicapped parking', where it appears on signs.
nuance.usage_note: Americans now prefer 'disabled' or 'person with a disability' when talking about people. 'Handicapped' still appears on signs, such as 'handicapped parking', and in older or legal contexts, though 'accessible' is increasingly used. Using it for a person may sound dated or unkind.

distinctions.note: Disabled is the current preferred American term for people, and it matches legal and everyday usage.
Impaired is more clinical and narrower, often describing a specific function such as vision or hearing.
Differently abled is considered a euphemism by many people with disabilities, so use disabled instead.

examples.everyday: The store's accessible entrance is around the side, near the loading dock, if you need it.
examples.professional: Our building inspection flagged two handicapped-accessible restrooms that lacked proper signage.
examples.analytical: Advocates have pushed to replace handicapped with disabled, because the older term frames disability as a personal limitation rather than a social barrier.

nuance.etymology: From 'handicap', whose origin is disputed but is popularly linked to a hand-in-cap betting game, extended to mean disadvantage.
common_mistakes: Calling a person 'handicapped' in American life when 'disabled' is preferred
Putting the stress on 'cap' instead of the first syllable

senses.definition: Food, especially meat and potatoes, chopped and mixed together. corn-beef hash.
A confused mess.
senses.example: After the team's reorganization, the project schedule became a complete hash of conflicting deadlines.

senses.definition: The # symbol (octothorpe, pound).
senses.example: Press the hash key on your phone to confirm the entry.

senses.definition: The result generated by a hash function.
senses.example: The server compares the file's hash to the stored value to detect tampering.

senses.definition: One guess made by a mining computer in the effort of finding the correct answer which releases the next unit of cryptocurrency; see also hashrate.
senses.example: His rig produced another hash every second, though only one in trillions would win the block.

senses.definition: A new mixture of old material; a second preparation or exhibition; a rehashing.
senses.example: The new album is mostly a hash of songs from their last two records.

senses.definition: A hash run.
Hashish, a drug derived from the cannabis plant.
senses.example: Police found a small bag of hash hidden inside the car's spare tire.

senses.definition: To chop into small pieces, to make into a hash.
senses.example: Hash the potatoes and onions into small cubes before frying them in the skillet.

senses.definition: To make a quick, rough version.
senses.example: We need to quickly hash up some plans.

senses.definition: To transform according to a hash function.
senses.example: The script hashes each password before storing it in the database.

senses.definition: To make a mess of (something); to ruin.
senses.example: The rainy weekend hashed our camping plans, so we stayed home watching movies.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of hash noise.

core.definition: Chopped meat and potatoes fried together, as in corned beef hash, a common diner breakfast dish.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with the short a of 'cat' and a clear sh at the end. Do not let the vowel drift toward 'hah' or add an extra uh after the sh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the food; 'make a hash of it' is negative, meaning to bungle or ruin something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans know 'hash' well from diners, where corned beef hash and hash browns are standard breakfast items. In office talk, 'hash out' means to discuss a problem thoroughly until it is settled, and in technology 'hash' also names the # symbol and a data-scrambling function. The food sense is casual, so ordering it at a diner sounds completely natural.

distinctions.note: Stew simmers in liquid until tender, while hash is chopped small and usually fried, giving it a crisp, browned texture.
'Mess' is a general word for disorder; 'make a hash of it' is more informal and implies bungling a task.
Both mean discussing something until it is resolved; 'hash out' is more casual and common in office talk, while 'thrash out' sounds more intense.

examples.everyday: I'll have the corned beef hash with two eggs over easy, please.
examples.professional: The caterer confirmed forty orders of hash for the morning breakfast, so we need more skillets.
examples.analytical: Corned beef hash is a dish of leftovers, which explains its origins in thrift and its lasting place on American diner menus.

nuance.analogy: Hash is a stew that was chopped up and fried instead of simmered, so every ingredient keeps its own crisp edge.
nuance.etymology: From French hachis ('chopped meat'), from hacher ('to chop'), related to hache ('axe').
common_mistakes: Saying 'make hash of it' without the article; the usual phrase is 'make a hash of it'.
Saying 'hash' for the # key on a phone call without context; Americans usually say 'pound' or 'the pound sign' when speaking about phone keypads.

hash.etymology: From French *hacher* (“to chop”), from Middle French *hacher*, from Old French *hacher*, from Old French *hache* (“axe”), from **happjā* (“axe”).

senses.definition: Thermal energy.
senses.example: This furnace puts out 5000 BTUs of heat. That engine is really throwing off some heat. Removal of heat from the liquid caused it to turn into a solid.

senses.definition: Heating system; a system that raises the temperature of a room or building.
senses.example: I'm freezing; could you turn on the heat?

senses.definition: The output of a heating system.
senses.example: During the power outage we had no heat because the controls are electric. Older folks like more heat than the young.

senses.definition: The condition or quality of being hot.
senses.example: Stay out of the heat of the sun!

senses.definition: A hot spell.
senses.example: The children stayed indoors during this year's summer heat.

senses.definition: An attribute of a spice that causes a burning sensation in the mouth.
senses.example: The chili sauce gave the dish heat.

senses.definition: A period of intensity, particularly of emotion.
senses.example: It's easy to make bad decisions in the heat of the moment.

senses.definition: An undesirable amount of attention.
senses.example: The heat from her family after her DUI arrest was unbearable.

senses.definition: A condition in which a mammal is aroused sexually or where it is especially fertile and therefore eager to mate.
senses.example: The male canines were attracted by the female in heat.

senses.definition: In omegaverse fiction, a cyclical period in which omegas experience an intense, sometimes irresistible biological urge to mate.
senses.example: In her omegaverse story, the heat forces the omega to seek out an alpha for protection.

senses.definition: The sexual arousal of a person, likened to that of a mammal.
senses.example: Their first date was charged with heat that neither of them could deny.

senses.definition: Semi-softcore NSFW art, primarily when posted to video-sharing websites.
senses.example: Her account was suspended after she uploaded too much heat to the video site.

senses.definition: A preliminary race, used to determine the participants in a final race.
senses.example: The runner had high hopes, but was out of contention after the first heat.

senses.definition: A stage in a competition, not necessarily a sporting one; a round.
senses.example: The defending champion was eliminated in the second heat of the regional chess tournament.

senses.definition: One cycle of bringing metal to maximum temperature and working it until it is too cool to work further.
senses.example: I can make a scroll like that in a single heat.

senses.definition: A violent action unintermitted; a single effort.
senses.example: The bull charged the fence in one furious heat before the rancher could react.

senses.definition: The police.
senses.example: The heat! Scram!

senses.definition: One or more firearms.
senses.example: Keep your hands where I can see them, and nobody gets hurt if nobody brings heat.

senses.definition: Stylish and valuable sneakers.
senses.example: Whoa, that guy is rocking some serious heat.

senses.definition: A negative reaction from the audience, especially as a heel (or bad character), or in general.
senses.example: The crowd gave the villain such a loud heat that the announcer could barely be heard.

senses.definition: A fastball.
senses.example: The catcher called for the heat, high and tight.

senses.definition: To cause an increase in temperature of (an object or space); to cause to become hot.
senses.example: I'll heat up the water.

senses.definition: To become hotter.
senses.example: There's a pot of soup heating on the stove.

senses.definition: To excite or make hot by action or emotion; to make feverish.
senses.example: Standing over the stove for hours had heated the kitchen until everyone felt feverish.

senses.definition: To excite ardor in; to rouse to action; to excite to excess; to inflame, as the passions.
senses.example: Her fiery speech heated the crowd's anger until the protest turned into a riot.

senses.definition: To arouse, to excite (sexually).
senses.example: The massage heated her up.

core.definition: The quality of being hot; thermal energy that flows from a warmer object to a cooler one.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single long vowel, so say a clean, long 'ee' with no glide. Do not shorten it to the 'ih' of 'hit.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It can feel negative in discomfort or pressure contexts, such as 'the heat of the summer' or 'the heat is on.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'heat' constantly for both temperature and home heating, as in 'Turn up the heat, it's freezing.' In the US, the home heating system is simply 'the heat,' while British speakers say 'central heating.' As a verb, Americans say 'heat up' for making food or a room warmer.

distinctions.note: Warmth describes a pleasant, mild temperature or kindness, while heat describes a higher, often intense temperature.
Temperature is a measurement of how hot something is, while heat is the energy that flows and changes that temperature.

collocations: in the heat of the moment

examples.everyday: Could you turn the heat down a little before the soup boils over?
examples.professional: Our cooling load rises sharply when server heat builds up during peak processing hours.
examples.analytical: Heat differs from work in that it flows only because of a temperature difference between two systems.

nuance.analogy: Heat is like water flowing downhill: it moves naturally from the higher level to the lower one until both are the same.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hǣtu, from the same root as 'hot,' meaning the state of being hot.
common_mistakes: Using 'heat' as an adjective: say 'It's hot outside,' not 'It's heat outside.'
Saying 'I have heat' to mean 'I feel hot'; Americans would say 'I'm hot' or 'I'm overheated.'

heat.etymology: From Middle English *hete*, from Old English *hǣtu*, from **haitī*, from Proto-Germanic **haitį̄* (“heat”), from Proto-Indo-European **keHy-* (“heat; hot”).

senses.definition: A group of seven world-creating archons (supernatural beings) often regarded as somewhat hostile; also, a term of address for the Demiurge (“a being sometimes seen as the creator of evil”).
senses.example: The gnostic text describes a hebdomad of archons who opposed the soul's ascent.

senses.definition: (historical) A period of seven days; a week.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A group or period of seven, especially a period of seven days; a week. This is a formal or historical term.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, HEB. The letters 'bd' are pronounced together, with a short schwa vowel in the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a learned, formal word that sounds scholarly or old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'hebdomad' in everyday speech, and they say 'week' or 'seven days' instead. You will see it in academic history, classical studies, and theology, especially in discussions of Gnostic cosmologies. Using it casually may sound pretentious, so reserve it for writing or formal settings.

distinctions.note: 'Week' is the ordinary everyday word. 'Hebdomad' is formal and emphasizes the number seven.
'Heptad' is a general word for a group of seven. 'Hebdomad' is used especially for seven days or for the seven Gnostic archons.

examples.professional: The report covers one hebdomad of trading data, running from Monday morning to the following Sunday.
examples.analytical: Gnostic cosmologies describe a hebdomad of archons who rule below the highest God and govern the material world.

nuance.analogy: Like a dozen eggs is a set of twelve, a hebdomad is a set of seven, most often a week.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hebdomas, 'the number seven'.
common_mistakes: Using 'hebdomad' in casual conversation where 'week' is expected.
Confusing 'hebdomad' with the adjective 'hebdomadal', which describes something weekly.

hebdomad.etymology: From Late Latin *hebdomada* (“number seven; group of seven; seven days”), *hebdomas* (“number seven; seven days; seventh day”), from Ancient Greek *ἑβδομάς* (“group of seven, especially seven days or seven years”), from *ἕβδομος* (“seventh”) + *-ᾰ́ς*.

senses.definition: History seen as the work of God's salvation. (Especially, in Christianity, the history of the Old Testament, seen as a preparation for the coming of Christ.)
senses.example: Her seminar on Heilsgeschichte traced how Israel's story prepared the way for Christ.

senses.definition: Any interpretation of history as leading to eventual well-being, as e.g. in Marxism.
senses.example: Her economics professor treated history as a Heilsgeschichte moving inevitably toward a classless society.

core.definition: In theology, the history of God's saving acts, viewed as an unfolding plan of salvation through events in time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HILE. The German 'ch' in the last syllables is a soft throat sound, which Americans usually replace with a plain 'k' or 'h' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a specialized term used in theological and biblical scholarship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Heilsgeschichte almost only in seminary classes, academic theology, and scholarly writing about Old Testament and New Testament interpretation. In ordinary church conversation people say 'salvation history' instead. Use the German term when you want to signal technical precision, and explain it briefly if your audience may not know it.

distinctions.note: Salvation history is the English equivalent and is more common in American churches and classrooms. Heilsgeschichte is the German technical term and often signals a specific scholarly school of thought.
Providence refers to God's continuing care and governance of the world. Heilsgeschichte focuses on the narrative sequence of God's redemptive acts through time.
A philosophy of history is a general theory of historical meaning, often secular. Heilsgeschichte is specifically theological, centered on God's saving purpose.

examples.everyday: My pastor said that the Bible tells one big story of salvation, which is what scholars call salvation history.
examples.professional: In the seminar we compared how two commentaries treat the Exodus within the larger Heilsgeschichte framework.
examples.analytical: Oscar Cullmann's account of Heilsgeschichte places the death and resurrection of Christ at the center of a linear sequence of divine acts in history.

nuance.analogy: Think of a novel in which every earlier chapter sets up the ending: Heilsgeschichte reads the Bible as that kind of story, with God's purpose unfolding chapter by chapter toward redemption.
nuance.etymology: From German Heil (salvation, wholeness) and Geschichte (history), a theological term developed in nineteenth-century German biblical scholarship.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ch' as a hard 'k' sound throughout, which marks it as clearly German and may sound odd in English conversation.
Using Heilsgeschichte as a general word for any history, rather than for the history of God's saving work.

senses.definition: The act of giving aid or assistance (to).
senses.example: She finds great joy in helping people.

senses.definition: A portion or serving, especially of food that one takes for oneself, or to which one helps oneself.
senses.example: She eagerly took a second helping of ice cream.

senses.definition: An amount or quantity.
senses.example: I'd like another helping of your mom's lasagna, please.

senses.definition: Helpful.
senses.example: The helping neighbors brought casseroles and offered rides every single day that week.

core.definition: A portion of food served to one person, especially a second helping that you take for yourself at the table.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The p is quick and is followed by the -ing sound, so don't add an extra vowel between the p and the ng.

nuance.connotation: Positive when food is offered generously. A 'second helping' is a welcome compliment to the cook.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Would you like another helping?' at home or with family. Restaurants usually say 'portion' or 'serving' on menus. 'Helping' in the aid sense is more formal and literary, so it is less common in daily speech.

distinctions.note: Serving is the general word used on menus and by restaurants, while helping is what you take at the table.
Portion is neutral and often used for measured or commercial amounts, while helping is more personal and home-like.
A plate is the dish you eat from, while a helping is the amount of food you put on it.

examples.everyday: Grandma insisted I have a second helping of her pot roast.
examples.professional: The caterer planned one helping of salad per guest, so we don't need to order extra for the reception.
examples.analytical: Discussions of distributive justice often ask what counts as a fair helping of resources for each member of society.

nuance.analogy: Like a slice of a shared pie: each person takes a helping, and the pie gets smaller.
nuance.etymology: From help; the food sense comes from the older use of helping someone to food at table.
common_mistakes: Confusing the food sense with the aid sense. 'A helping of potatoes' is food, while 'a helping hand' means assistance.
Dropping the p in pronunciation and saying 'hel-ing'. Keep the p clear.

senses.definition: An inheritance; property that may be inherited.
A tradition; a practice or set of values that is passed down from preceding generations through families or through institutional memory.
A birthright; the status acquired by birth, especially of but not exclusive to the firstborn.
senses.example: By custom, the title was his heritage, passed down to him at birth as the firstborn.

senses.definition: Having a certain background, such as growing up with a second language.
senses.example: a heritage speaker; a heritage language

core.definition: Traditions, values, customs, or property passed down from earlier generations, such as a family's or a nation's cultural legacy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The -age ending is unstressed and sounds like 'ij'. The middle t between vowels is often flapped to a soft d sound, so it sounds like 'HAIR-uh-dij'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, suggesting pride, continuity and respect for the past; it can sound grand when used about institutions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heritage for cultural background, as in Hispanic Heritage Month, and for historic places, as in heritage site or heritage railroad. It is a little more formal than 'background' or 'roots'. In casual talk people say 'my family's heritage' or 'Irish heritage', but would not call a single family recipe a heritage unless speaking with some weight.

distinctions.note: A tradition is any custom passed on, while heritage is broader and emphasizes what a group values as its shared history.
An inheritance is usually money or property received after someone dies, while heritage often refers to cultural or historical identity.
A legacy is what a person leaves behind through actions or gifts, while heritage is what a group receives from the past.

examples.everyday: We're going to the Korean festival this weekend to celebrate our family's heritage.
examples.professional: We're replacing the old reporting tools, but we're keeping the company's heritage of careful documentation.
examples.analytical: A community's heritage is not only a set of relics but a continuing argument about which inherited practices deserve to continue.

nuance.analogy: Like a family recipe passed down through generations, changed a little by each cook who makes it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French heritage, from heriter 'to inherit', from Latin hereditare.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable as in 'heri-TAGE', which is wrong; the stress is on the first syllable.
Using heritage to mean a single inherited object, when inheritance is the better word for property.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses the idea of heritage for land and for a people's special place before God. The Hebrew word nahalah means inheritance, possession, or portion, often of land. In Psalm 127:3 children are described as a heritage from the LORD, and in Psalm 16:6 the psalmist says he has a goodly heritage. Both passages show heritage as a gift that comes from God rather than something earned.

heritage.etymology: From Middle English *heritage*, from Old French *eritage,heritage*, ultimately derived from Latin *hērēs*.

senses.definition: The political subjection of a community to the rule of another power or to an external law.
senses.example: Under colonial heteronomy, the island's courts answered to officials across the ocean.

senses.definition: The state of being beholden to external influences.
The condition of being heteronomous.

core.definition: The condition of being governed by an external law, power, or influence rather than by one's own self-given law.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on RAH, the third syllable, with a reduced vowel in the last two syllables. The final -y is a clear ee sound. Keep the r clear in the middle of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, but can carry a negative tone when used to criticize external control.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heteronomy in philosophy, theology, and political theory, usually in discussions of Kant or of human freedom. It is rare in everyday speech, where people would say control by others. In academic writing it is often paired with autonomy to show a contrast.

distinctions.note: Autonomy is self-rule or self-direction, while heteronomy is the condition of being ruled by an outside power or law.
Subjugation is the forceful conquest of a people, while heteronomy can refer to a more abstract or moral dependence on external authority.

examples.professional: The policy team argued that the new rules created heteronomy, because local offices had no say in how the standards were applied.
examples.analytical: Christian anthropologists have often asked whether the human will is truly free when it lives under the heteronomy of sin rather than the self-giving of grace.

nuance.analogy: Heteronomy is like a house built on someone else's land: you live there, but the rules of the property come from outside you.
nuance.etymology: From Greek heteronomia (subjection to another's law), from heteronomos, from heteros (other) and nomos (law).
common_mistakes: Using heteronomy as a general word for being controlled; it has a specific philosophical meaning about external law.
Confusing it with heterogeneity, which refers to mixed composition.

senses.definition: Of very good quality; superior.
senses.example: She always wears high-quality clothes.

core.definition: Of very good quality; superior, reliable, and well made.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KWAH, and the word has three quick syllables with a reduced middle vowel. In General American, the vowel in KWAH is the same as in 'cot,' which is often merged with 'caught.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies excellence and value, and sometimes that the item is worth paying for.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective in shopping, business, food, and product descriptions, as in 'This is a high-quality knife.' It is very common in everyday speech and writing. In a sales context, people often say 'premium' or 'top-quality' for emphasis, and in casual talk they may simply say 'really good.'

distinctions.note: Top-quality means the best available, while high-quality means very good but not necessarily the very best.
Premium emphasizes a higher price and special status, while high-quality focuses on the actual standard of the product.

examples.everyday: That bakery uses high-quality flour, so their bread tastes much better than the grocery store bread.
examples.professional: We need to deliver high-quality data to the model team, so the validation pipeline must catch missing values early.
examples.analytical: A high-quality argument does more than cite authorities; it tests its premises against the strongest objections.

nuance.analogy: High-quality work is like a well-built bridge: you do not notice it carrying heavy loads, but you trust it every day.
nuance.etymology: From high plus quality, from Latin qualitas, from qualis, 'of what kind.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel in KWAH like 'kwah-ee' or 'kway,' rather than the American 'KWAH.'
Using high-quality as a noun, as in 'the high-quality,' which is not standard.

senses.definition: At an important, elevated, or exalted level in a hierarchy or organization; high-level.
senses.example: She is a high-ranking official in the government.

core.definition: Holding a senior or important position in a formal hierarchy, such as a government, military, or corporation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on RANK, with 'high' getting lighter secondary stress. Use a short a like in 'bank', and keep the -nk sound clean instead of adding an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes rank without judging the person, though it can suggest privilege when used with power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for officials, officers, executives, and senior members of an organization, especially in news reports and workplace talk. It is more formal than 'senior' in everyday speech and more specific about hierarchy than 'important.' A natural reply to someone describing a person this way is simply 'Oh, really?' or asking what their role is.

distinctions.note: Senior often refers to length of service or a job grade, while high-ranking stresses formal authority in a chain of command.
Prominent means well known or noticeable, and a prominent person need not hold any official position.
Powerful describes influence over outcomes, which a high-ranking person may or may not have in practice.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's brother is a high-ranking officer in the Navy, so he's always traveling.
examples.professional: The compliance report must be reviewed by a high-ranking executive before it goes to the board.
examples.analytical: Decisions made by high-ranking officials often reflect institutional incentives more than individual judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like the top floors of a skyscraper, where access is limited to those with the highest clearance.
nuance.etymology: Rank comes from Old French ranc, meaning row or line; high comes from Old English heah.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'ranking' on the second syllable as 'ran-KING' instead of RANK-ing.
Using 'high-ranking' for a high score or grade, which is not a hierarchy.

senses.definition: A cocktail made from a spirit plus soda water etc.
senses.example: The bartender poured a tall highball of bourbon and ginger ale for the professor.

senses.definition: An all clear or full speed ahead signal.
senses.example: The conductor gave the highball signal, and the freight train rolled out of the yard.

senses.definition: A very high bouldering problem, often with a hard landing.
senses.example: The climber struggled up the highball, a tall boulder problem with a dangerous landing on the pads.

senses.definition: Clipping of highball glass, a tall glass tumbler used for serving highballs.
senses.example: She set the sparkling water in a chilled highball glass beside the lime wedge.

senses.definition: To make an estimate which tends toward exaggeration.
senses.example: If we highball the price, it comes out to $240. If we lowball it, it's closer to $200.

senses.definition: To move quickly; to hightail.
senses.example: When the storm rolled in, the hikers highballed back down the trail toward the parking lot.

core.definition: A tall drink of liquor, such as whiskey or gin, mixed with soda water or ginger ale and served over ice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HY, the first syllable. The second syllable uses the open vowel of 'cot,' so it sounds like 'bahl,' not 'bowl.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a casual bar term and does not carry strong positive or negative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans order a highball at bars and restaurants, often naming the spirit, as in 'a whiskey highball' or 'a gin highball.' It is a classic, simple drink that is more common in older bars than in trendy cocktail lounges. As a verb, highball is informal and means to hurry away, and it is rarely used in modern speech.

distinctions.note: Cocktail is the general term for mixed drinks, while a highball is one specific style made with a spirit and a carbonated mixer.
On the rocks means served over ice, which can be done with almost any drink, while highball refers to the mixing style.
Neat means a spirit served plain with no ice or mixer, which is the opposite of a highball.

examples.everyday: I'll have a whiskey highball, please, with a lot of ice.
examples.professional: Let's book the back room at the steakhouse for the team dinner, since they make a good highball.
examples.analytical: The highball, a simple mix of spirit and carbonated water, reflects the bar culture of mid-twentieth-century America.

nuance.analogy: Like a lighter, bubbly cousin of a cocktail, tall and refreshing on a hot day.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'bowl' instead of 'bahl.'
Using highball to mean any mixed drink, when it refers to a specific tall style of drink.

highball.etymology: From *high* + *ball*, of the same railroad origins as *lowball*.

senses.definition: To make higher; to raise or increase in amount or quantity.
senses.example: The bank decided to higher its interest rates again after inflation rose in March.

senses.definition: To ascend.
senses.example: We watched the glider higher above the valley until it vanished into the clouds.

core.definition: Greater in level, amount, degree or rank than something else; further above the ground or a baseline.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the second syllable is a reduced, r-colored vowel, not a separate 'ayr' sound. Say it as one smooth word, 'HY-er'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes measurable level, amount or rank without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use higher for amounts, levels and ranks: higher prices, a higher floor, a higher score. For a person's stature, Americans say taller. The Scottish exam sense (the Higher) is mainly British or Scottish; Americans speak of college entrance exams such as the SAT or ACT. The verb sense 'to raise' is rare in American speech, where people say raise or increase.

distinctions.note: Taller describes stature or the height of people, trees and buildings; higher describes level, position or amount.
Upper describes the position of one part within a set (the upper floor); higher suggests a greater degree or level.
Greater describes size or magnitude in general; higher is used for vertical position, levels and rates.

examples.everyday: Our son is applying to college next year, and he's hoping for higher scores on the SAT.
examples.professional: Can we set a higher target for the third-quarter conversion rate?
examples.analytical: A higher standard of evidence is required when a claim contradicts well-established findings.

nuance.analogy: Like rungs on a ladder: each one is higher than the one below, measured by level rather than by how tall a person is.
nuance.etymology: From Old English heah, 'high', with the comparative suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Saying 'more higher' (a double comparative); use 'higher' alone.
Saying 'higher' for a person's height; say 'taller'.

senses.definition: A graphical display of numerical data in the form of upright bars, with the area of each bar representing frequency.
senses.example: The histogram showed that most customers spent between twenty and forty dollars per visit.

senses.definition: To represent (data) as a histogram.
senses.example: Before modeling, I histogram the residuals to check whether they look roughly normal.

core.definition: A bar chart that shows how many data values fall into each range, where the bars touch and their heights show frequency.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HIS, and the second syllable is a weak 'tuh'. Learners often stress the last syllable or pronounce the 'o' in the middle as a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; the word has no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American data science, statistics and business reporting, histogram is a standard term that people use with colleagues and in presentations. It differs from a bar chart in that the bars touch and represent continuous or binned numerical data. Americans may say 'bar graph' loosely, but for distribution plots 'histogram' is the correct term.

distinctions.note: A bar chart compares separate categories with gaps between bars; a histogram shows frequencies of numerical ranges with touching bars.
A density plot shows a smooth curve estimating the distribution; a histogram shows discrete bins of frequencies.

examples.everyday: My daughter's school project was a histogram of how many hours each kid spent on homework.
examples.professional: Before we fit the model, let's plot a histogram of the response variable to check for skew.
examples.analytical: A histogram conveys the empirical distribution, but the chosen bin width can change how we perceive its shape.

nuance.analogy: A histogram is like sorting marbles into labeled cups by size and then comparing how full each cup is.
nuance.etymology: Coined from Greek histos ('upright post' or 'mast') and gramma ('drawing'), and popularized by Karl Pearson in 1895.
common_mistakes: Calling any bar chart a histogram; in a histogram the bars touch and represent numerical ranges.
Stressing the second syllable, saying 'his-TOG-ruh-m'.

histogram.etymology: Probably from Ancient Greek *ἱστός* (“mast”) + *γράμμα*, although it is sometimes claimed to have been derived from *historical* + *diagram*; coined in 1891 by English mathematician Karl Pearson.

senses.definition: A structure, whether artificial or natural, for housing a swarm of honeybees.
senses.example: The beekeeper inspected each hive carefully before the spring honey harvest began.

senses.definition: The bees of one hive; a swarm of bees.
senses.example: The hive swarmed out of the old oak tree and settled on a low branch.

senses.definition: A place swarming with busy occupants; a crowd.
senses.example: The after-school club became a busy hive of kids painting posters and shouting ideas.

senses.definition: A section of the registry.
senses.example: The archivist moved the old tax records into the hive reserved for pre-1950 filings.

senses.definition: An itchy, red, swollen area of the skin; singular or attributive form of hives.
senses.example: She took an antihistamine for the hive that spread across her neck after lunch.

senses.definition: To collect (bees) into a hive.
senses.example: to hive a swarm of bees

senses.definition: To store (something other than bees) in, or as if in, a hive.
senses.example: She hived away her savings in a single fund and rarely checked on it.

senses.definition: To form a hive-like entity.
senses.example: Within hours, the dispersed bacteria began to hive into a single dense colony.

senses.definition: To take lodging or shelter together; to reside in a collective body.
senses.example: Several retired teachers hived together in one shared house near the old university.

senses.definition: Of insects: to enter or possess a hive.
senses.example: Bees hived in the wall cavity of our garage over the winter.

core.definition: A box or structure where honeybees live and make honey, or the colony of bees living inside it.

pronunciation.tip: Use the long 'i' diphthong as in 'five' and end with a voiced 'v'. Do not devoice the final sound to 'f', as in 'hife'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In the phrase 'hive of activity' it is positive, suggesting energy and busyness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hive' for beekeeping and for busy places, such as 'This office is a hive of activity.' In everyday speech, 'beehive' is equally common for the bee structure. Americans rarely use 'hive' for a single bee; they say 'a bee' or 'a colony of bees'.

distinctions.note: Beehive means the same thing and is the more common everyday term; hive is also common and slightly more technical.
A colony is the biological group of bees; a hive is the structure that houses them.
A swarm is a group of bees leaving the hive to form a new colony, not the hive itself.

examples.everyday: My neighbor keeps a hive in her backyard, and every fall she gives us jars of honey.
examples.professional: The startup office is a hive of activity every morning before the first stand-up meeting.
examples.analytical: The bee hive is often used as a metaphor for collective intelligence, though the comparison hides how individual workers differ.

nuance.analogy: A hive is like a busy airport terminal where every worker has a specific role.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'hȳf', meaning a basket or beehive.
common_mistakes: Using 'hive' to mean a single bee; a hive is the house for a whole colony.
Pronouncing it as a short vowel, like 'hiv'; the vowel is long, as in 'five'.

hive.etymology: From Middle English *hyve*, from Old English *hȳf*, from **hūfi*, from Proto-Indo-European **kuHp-* (“water vessel”), from **kew-* (“to bend, curve”).

senses.definition: In a homeomorphic manner.

core.definition: In a way that relates two spaces or structures through a homeomorphism, preserving their topological properties.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on MOR, as in homeomorphic. The ending -ically is pronounced -ik-lee, with a short vowel and no strong syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It belongs to mathematical writing and is rarely used outside it.
nuance.usage_note: Use homeomorphically only in technical writing or talks about topology. Students and researchers in American math departments use it to describe how spaces correspond. In casual speech, people would just say that two shapes are basically the same.

distinctions.note: Isomorphically is the general structure-preserving adverb in many fields, while homeomorphically is specific to topology.

examples.everyday: My son's math homework asked whether two shapes correspond homeomorphically, and I had to look it up.
examples.professional: The proof shows the two manifolds are related homeomorphically, so the invariants carry over.
examples.analytical: We can transfer the property only if the mapping works homeomorphically, preserving open sets in both directions.

nuance.analogy: Like two rubber shapes that can be molded into each other without cutting.
nuance.etymology: From homeomorphic, from Greek homoios, similar, and morphē, form, plus the adverbial -ally.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adverb with the noun homeomorphism when a verb or adverb is needed.
Mispronouncing the -ically ending as -ical-ly with a strong vowel.

senses.definition: The state of being sexually and romantically attracted primarily or exclusively to persons of the same sex, sometimes restricted to same-sex attraction between males.
Sexual activity with a person of the same sex, sometimes restricted to same-sex sex between males.
senses.example: Many state laws once criminalized homosexuality, a fact the textbook discusses in its chapter on civil rights.

core.definition: The condition of being romantically and sexually attracted mainly or only to people of the same sex. Often used as a neutral, formal term.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the AL in the final part, with a light secondary stress on SEK. The -sual- part reduces to 'shoo', and the final -ity ends as a reduced 'ih-tee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic and medical contexts, but it can sound clinical or loaded in everyday talk. Many Americans prefer gay, lesbian or bisexual when describing people, and reserve homosexuality for discussing the orientation as a general topic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use homosexuality mainly in formal writing, research, policy, religious debate and news reporting. In casual talk, people usually say gay or talk about someone's sexual orientation. Using homosexual as a noun for a person now sounds dated or clinical to many people, so describe people as gay or lesbian instead.

distinctions.note: Sexual orientation is the broader umbrella term covering attraction to men, women, both or neither, while homosexuality names one specific pattern of same-sex attraction.
Gay is a common, informal identity term used mostly for people, and it is the usual choice in everyday American speech, while homosexuality is more formal and analytical.

examples.everyday: My aunt and uncle are pretty open-minded, and they never made a big deal about homosexuality when my cousin came out.
examples.professional: Our HR training now covers discrimination based on sexual orientation, including homosexuality, so managers know what protections apply.
examples.analytical: Historians dispute whether the modern category of homosexuality can be applied to premodern societies without distorting how people understood desire and identity.

nuance.analogy: Like a label on a map: useful for describing a region, but it can flatten the complicated terrain of real people's lives.
nuance.etymology: Formed from Greek homo- (same) and Latin sexus (sex), with the English suffix -ity; the term was coined in the late 1800s.
common_mistakes: Using homosexuality to refer to a person, as in 'He is a homosexuality'; say 'He is gay' or 'He is a gay man'.
Stressing the wrong syllable; the strongest stress is on the AL, not on SEX.
nuance.biblical_note: The word itself does not appear in the Bible, and it postdates the Bible by many centuries. The RSV uses the word homosexuals in 1 Corinthians 6:9 to translate the Greek term arsenokoitai, which refers to men who lie with males; a related term appears in 1 Timothy 1:10. Leviticus 18:22 (Hebrew to'ebah, abomination) forbids a man lying with a male as with a woman, and Romans 1:26-27 describes same-sex relations as contrary to nature in a passage about humanity turning away from God. Scholars debate how these texts should be interpreted, especially the meaning of arsenokoitai and the social practices the texts address.

traditions.view: Orthodox teaching holds that sexual intimacy belongs within marriage between a man and a woman, so same-sex sexual activity is regarded as sinful. The Church also calls for compassion, pastoral care and welcome for people who experience same-sex attraction.

The Catechism distinguishes between the inclination, which it does not call sinful in itself, and homosexual acts, which it calls intrinsically disordered. It asks that homosexual persons be treated with respect, compassion and sensitivity, and be called to chastity.

Views differ widely. Many evangelical, Reformed and conservative churches teach that same-sex sexual relations are sinful, while several mainline Lutheran, Methodist, Presbyterian, Anglican and United Church bodies have increasingly affirmed committed same-sex relationships, and debate continues within each tradition.

senses.definition: Tending to impair or damage; injurious; occasioning loss or injury.
senses.example: The new tariffs proved hurtful to small farmers who relied on export markets.

senses.definition: Tending to hurt someone's feelings; insulting; lacerating.
senses.example: Her hurtful comment about my accent stung long after the party ended.

core.definition: Causing emotional pain, such as remarks that insult or wound someone's feelings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, HURT, and the ending -ful is reduced to a weak fuhl. Keep the r clear and do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes words or actions that cause emotional pain, often unintentionally.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hurtful mainly for words, comments or actions that wound feelings, as in a hurtful remark. It is common in everyday talk and in advice about relationships. For physical harm, use harmful or injurious.

distinctions.note: Harmful is broader and often refers to physical or practical damage, while hurtful is mainly emotional.
Cruel implies deliberate unkindness, while hurtful can describe a remark that was careless.

examples.everyday: That was a hurtful thing to say, even if you were joking.
examples.professional: Please avoid hurtful comments in the feedback meeting, and focus on the work.
examples.analytical: A hurtful statement can undermine trust even when its literal content is accurate.

nuance.analogy: Like a splinter under the skin, small but hard to ignore once it is there.
common_mistakes: Using hurtful for physical injuries, as in a hurtful fall, where injurious or harmful is more natural
Pronouncing the second syllable as FOOL with full stress

senses.definition: Any function that is a solution of the hypergeometric equation; usually an expansion of an hypergeometric series.

core.definition: A special mathematical function, usually written as a hypergeometric series, that solves a particular second-order differential equation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress in the adjective falls on MET, and in the phrase the noun 'function' is stressed on FUNGK. Pronounce the 'ction' ending as 'kshun,' with the 'k' sound clearly heard.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: This is a specialized term from advanced mathematics and mathematical physics. Americans encounter it in graduate courses, numerical computing, and research. Non-specialists would just say 'a special function,' so use the full phrase only with people who work in math or physics.

distinctions.note: The function is the value it produces, while the series is one way to write the function as an infinite sum.
Elementary functions such as sine and exponential are simpler, while hypergeometric functions form a much broader class that includes them as special cases.

collocations: hypergeometric function of a complex variable

examples.everyday: I heard a physics professor mention a hypergeometric function, and I had no idea what it was.
examples.professional: The numerical library lets us evaluate the hypergeometric function quickly for large parameters, which speeds up the model.
examples.analytical: The solution to the equation can be written as a hypergeometric function, which unifies many special functions under one formula.

nuance.analogy: A master formula that produces many other special functions as particular cases, like a general recipe that yields many specific dishes.
nuance.etymology: From the hypergeometric series, which generalizes the geometric series, from Greek hyper, 'beyond,' and geometria, 'measuring the earth.'
common_mistakes: Confusing the function with the series, when the series is only one representation of the function.
